greek_from_text: Bishop Antiochus of Resaina at the Council of Nicaea, 325. Theodosius I enlarged the town as Theodosiopolis, c. 380; the 3rd-c. colony coins of Septimius Severus are Latin.
until_text: Administration: taken in Iyad ibn Ghanm's conquest of the Jazira, 640 (al-Baladhuri). Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
ended_by: Taken, by some accounts by storm, in Iyad ibn Ghanm's conquest of the Jazira, 640 (al-Baladhuri). No named act ended Greek speech.
founder: Theodosius I (Theodosiopolis); earlier a colonia of Septimius Severus
pre_greek_note: Adjacent Tell Fakhariya is Iron Age Sikani (Assyrian-Aramaic bilingual statue); it is a separate mound, so its name is not given as Resaina's.
bilingual_evidence: a Roman colony and then a see with Greek-signing bishops in a Syriac-speaking region; Sergius of Reshaina (d. 536) translated Greek medicine and philosophy into Syriac
status_evidence: See of Osrhoene under Edessa: bishop Antiochus at Nicaea 325 and later bishops; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena; Roman colony (Septimius Severus).
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. Its people spoke Syriac; its native Sergius of Reshaina (d. 536) wrote in Syriac and translated from Greek. The ruins lie on the Syrian side of the border.
sources: Jones 1971; Pleiades 874662; Wikipedia: Ras al-Ayn

other_names: Rhesapha; Raṣappa (Akkadian); Reṣeph (Hebrew Bible); Anastasiopolis (under Anastasius); Rusafa, Rusafat Hisham (Arabic)
site: Resafa, south of the Euphrates, Raqqa Governorate
greek_from_text: the pilgrim town at the shrine of St Sergius got its first bishop shortly after 431 (from John of Antioch); city rank and metropolis under Anastasius (491-518)
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest after the Yarmuk, c. 637-639; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town stayed Christian and became the residence of the caliph Hisham (724-743). The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions into the later 6th c. Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest after the Yarmuk, c. 637-639. Earlier Khosrow I extorted its church treasures from bishop Candidus, 542 (Procopius, Wars 2.20).
pre_greek_note: An Assyrian provincial centre; the Roman fort and pilgrim town grew on or near it.
bilingual_evidence: Greek building and dedicatory inscriptions of the 5th-6th c.; Syriac-speaking clergy and Arab (Ghassanid) patrons of the shrine of St Sergius
status_evidence: see from c. 431; metropolis of Augusta Euphratensis under Anastasius; Procopius, Buildings 2.9
note: Bilingual rather than Greek: a pilgrim town of an Aramaic- and Arabic-speaking region with Greek as the written language.
sources: Fowden 1999; Procopius, Wars 2.20; Pleiades 668354; Wikipedia: Sergiopolis

site: Al-Suriyya, al-Suriyya, near al-Mansura, al-Thawrah District, Raqqa Governorate
greek_from_text: Bishop Uranius of Sura, for whom the metropolitan Stephen signed at Chalcedon, 451; the town was the base of legio XVI Flavia Firma.
until_text: Administration: finally taken in the Arab conquest of the Euphrates valley, 637/638. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
ended_by: Taken and burned by Khosrow I, who enslaved its people, 540 (Procopius, Wars 2.5); bishop Candidus of Sergiopolis tried to ransom 12,000 captives. Rebuilt by Justinian (Buildings 2.9). Finally taken in the Arab conquest, 637/638 (no commander recorded for the town).
bilingual_evidence: a see and a city in Procopius' narrative; Aramaic-speaking population
status_evidence: See of Augusta Euphratensis under Hierapolis (Notitia Antiochena): bishops Uranius (451) and Marius (deposed 518); an unnamed bishop in Procopius' account of 540; a city in Hierocles and Procopius (Wars 2.5).
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. Greek is otherwise attested only through its garrison, officials and bishops.
sources: Wikipedia: Sura, Syria; Procopius, Wars 2.5; Pleiades 668376

other_names: Tourmeda (Syrian name, Stephanus of Byzantium); Tiphsah? (Hebrew Bible)
site: an Euphrates crossing in north Syria; not securely located (sites proposed between Jerablus and Raqqa)
greek_from_text: Seleucus I refounded Thapsacus as Amphipolis (Pliny NH 5.87; Stephanus of Byzantium s.v. Amphipolis)
until_text: No record of the city after Pliny; the end of Greek speech there is unknown.
fade_evidence: Last mentioned as Amphipolis by Pliny (1st c. AD).
ended_by: No named act: the city disappears from the record after the 1st c. AD.
pre_greek_note: Tiphsah is commonly equated with Thapsacus, but the identification is not certain; Xenophon (Anab. 1.4.11) knew Thapsacus as a large city.
status_evidence: Appian Syr. 57 (Amphipolis among Seleucus I's cities); Pliny NH 5.87; Stephanus of Byzantium; Cohen 2006
note: The site is unlocated; the coordinates are Pleiades' rough placement.
sources: Cohen 2006, 184-186; Pliny NH 5.87; Pleiades 658377

site: Halabiye, on the right bank of the Euphrates, Deir ez-Zor Governorate
greek_from_text: Listed as a see under Sergiopolis in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570).
until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the Euphrates valley, 637-640. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the Euphrates valley, 637-640.
founder: Palmyra (under Zenobia, 3rd c.); rebuilt by Justinian
bilingual_evidence: A walled town of the Euphrates with a see of the Greek-speaking church in the 6th c.
status_evidence: See under the metropolis of Sergiopolis in the Notitia Antiochena; Procopius (Buildings 2.8) calls it a small city, walled anew by Justinian.
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. A fortified town founded under Palmyra and named after its queen; Greek building inscriptions of Justinian's works belong to the builders. No bishop is known by name.
sources: Procopius, Buildings 2.8; Wikipedia (it): Arcidiocesi di Sergiopoli; Pleiades 894185

other_names: Abila of Lysanias; Abilene (the tetrarchy, Luke 3:1)
site: Suq Wadi Barada, Wadi Barada, Rif Dimashq Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek dedication by Nymphaios, freedman of the tetrarch Lysanias, under Tiberius (OGIS 606); the town was the seat of the tetrarchy of Abilene
until_text: Administration passed to the Arabs with the Damascus region in 634-636. There is no later evidence for Greek speakers here; Aramaic survived in the nearby Qalamun villages. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
fade_evidence: Latin inscriptions of the road cut through the Barada gorge under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus at the expense of the Abilenes (CIL III 199-201); Greek inscriptions of residents; a see of Phoenice Libanensis in the 5th-6th centuries. Regional markers: flight of Roman inhabitants at the conquest and resettlement of the coast (al-Baladhuri); Greek in the registers until c. 700-707; Arabic Melkite writing by c. 800 (Theodore Abu Qurra).
ended_by: No named act: the town came under the Arabs with the Damascus region in Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign, 634-636; the evidence for Greek speakers ends then.
bilingual_evidence: Capital of an Ituraean tetrarchy with Semitic names in its Greek inscriptions; Greek dedications by residents from the reign of Tiberius; the Abilenes paid for the Roman road as a civic body (163-165)
status_evidence: Capital of the tetrarchy of Abilene (Josephus; Luke 3:1); Ptolemy 5.15; bishop's see of Phoenice Libanensis (Notitia Antiochena, Le Quien)
note: The local shrine of Nabi Habil ('Abel') preserves the name. Civic status in the Roman period rests on its role as tetrarchic capital and later see.
sources: OGIS 606; Josephus AJ 19.275, 20.138; Wikipedia: Abila Lysaniou; Pleiades 677993

other_names: Pella (name of the Macedonian settlement, Strabo 16.2.10); Pharnake (earlier name, Strabo); Chersonesos (Strabo); Afamiya (Arabic)
site: Qalaat al-Madiq, al-Suqaylabiyah District, Hama Governorate
greek_from_text: Seleucus I founded it c. 300 BC on the site of Pharnake, also called Pella, as the military and elephant base of the kingdom (Strabo 16.2.10)
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah in 637/638; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. Apamea had already been plundered by Khosrow I in 540 and burned, with its people deported, in 573. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
fade_evidence: Greek city inscriptions, mosaics and the Neoplatonist school (Numenius, Amelius) to the 3rd c.; Greek church inscriptions into the 6th c.; mass deportation by the Persians in 573 (Evagrius 5.10). Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
ended_by: Surrendered to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 637/638 (al-Baladhuri). Earlier blows: plundered by Khosrow I, 540 (Procopius, Wars 2.11); taken and burned by Khosrow I's general Adarmahan, who deported its people, 573 (Evagrius 5.10; John of Ephesus 6.6).
pre_greek_note: Pharnake is attested only in Greek (Strabo); the identification of the site with Bronze Age Niya (Akkadian, Egyptian) is disputed; the citadel tell has Bronze Age levels.
status_evidence: Strabo 16.2.10; city coins from the 2nd c. BC; metropolis of Syria Secunda; bishops from 325; Hierocles
sources: Cohen 2006, 94-101; Strabo 16.2.10; Grainger 1990; Pleiades 668335; Wikipedia: Apamea, Syria

other_names: Arastan (Middle Persian, Shapur I's inscription); al-Rastan (Arabic)
site: Al-Rastan, al-Rastan District, Homs Governorate
greek_from_text: listed by Appian (Syr. 57) among the cities Seleucus I named after places in Macedonia; c. 300 BC
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah in 637; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
ended_by: Surrendered to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 637 (al-Baladhuri). No named act ended Greek speech.
refounded_by: held by the Emesene dynasts (Sampsigeramus) in the 1st c. BC (Strabo 16.2.10)
status_evidence: Appian Syr. 57; Strabo 16.2.10; Roman city coins with Greek legends; see of Syria Secunda (Mark of Arethusa, 4th c.); Hierocles
note: Modern al-Rastan is generally held to continue the name Arethusa.
sources: Cohen 2006, 102-103; Appian, Syr. 57; Pleiades 668199; Wikipedia: Al-Rastan

site: Qara, Qalamoun, Rif Dimashq Governorate (proposed)
greek_from_text: Bishop Dadas of Chonochora, for whom the metropolitan Theodore of Damascus signed at Chalcedon (451); Dadas signed the letter of the bishops of Phoenice II to Leo I in 458.
until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the Damascus-Homs road, 634-636. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
fade_evidence: Last bishop known: Alexander, expelled in 518. Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the Damascus-Homs road, 634-636.
bilingual_evidence: A see of the Greek-speaking church under Damascus in the Aramaic-speaking Qalamoun.
status_evidence: See of Phoenice Libanensis under Damascus: bishop Dadas (451, 458); Alexander, a Miaphysite expelled in 518; Notitia Antiochena (c. 570). Identified with Qara (Wikipedia it, after Vailhe, Honigmann and Janin); 'Chonacara?' at Qara in the Barrington Atlas.
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The identification with Qara is usual but tentative in the Barrington Atlas. Corada, a separate see under Damascus, is not this place. Le Quien wrongly gave it three bishops of Carrhae (Harran).
sources: Wikipedia (it): Diocesi di Conocora; Pleiades 668221; Honigmann, BZ 25 (1925); Devreesse 1945

other_names: Demetrias (civic coins, c. 87-84 BC); Colonia Damascus (under Philip the Arab); Dimashq, al-Sham (Arabic)
site: Old City of Damascus, Damascus Governorate
greek_from_text: Civic bronze coins naming the city Demetrias, c. 87-84 BC (after Demetrius III, who ruled from Damascus 96-87 BC); before that a Ptolemaic and, from 200 BC, Seleucid stronghold with a royal mint (from 128 BC)
until_text: Administration: the city capitulated to the Arabs in 635 and was the Umayyad capital from 661; Greek stayed in the caliphal offices of Syria until the order to keep the registers in Arabic, c. 700-705 (al-Baladhuri). Speech: the Greek-speaking Melkite elite (the family of Mansur ibn Sarjun, John of Damascus) lasted into the 8th century; by the 9th century the Melkites of Damascus wrote and spoke Arabic.
fade_evidence: John of Damascus (c. 675-c. 750) wrote in Greek and served in the caliph's administration before retiring to Mar Saba; Andrew of Crete was born at Damascus c. 660; Peter, metropolitan of Damascus, had his tongue cut out and was exiled to Arabia Felix (Yemen) by al-Walid II, 743 (Theophanes AM 6234; Chronicle of 1234); a fragment of Psalm 77 in Arabic written in Greek letters, found in the Umayyad mosque, was first dated to the late 8th c. but is now placed in the late 9th or early 10th c., and shows Greek script used by Arabic-speaking Christians; Melkite writing turns to Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Pauline Epistles of Sinai Ar. 151, translated from Syriac by Bishr ibn al-Sirri at Damascus, 867).
ended_by: Taken by Khalid ibn al-Walid and Abu Ubayda after a siege, 635, and again after the battle of the Yarmuk, 636; Greek dropped from the registers by order of 'Abd al-Malik or al-Walid I, c. 700-705. No named act ended Greek speech, which faded with the Melkite shift to Arabic.
pre_greek_name: Dimašqa (Akkadian, Amarna letters); Tmśq (Egyptian, list of Thutmose III); Dammeśeq (Hebrew Bible); Darmeśeq (Aramaic)
bilingual_evidence: Aramaic was spoken in the city and its villages (Syriac and Christian Palestinian Aramaic texts); Arabic-speaking tribes in the hinterland; Greek was the civic and church language
status_evidence: Civic coins as Demetrias (c. 87-84 BC) and Roman city coins; listed in the Decapolis by Pliny (NH 5.74); Roman colonia; metropolis of Phoenice Libanensis; bishops at Nicaea 325 and later councils; Hierocles
note: Greek settlers were probably present earlier: the grid plan of the Old City is usually dated to the Hellenistic period, but the first civic evidence is the Demetrias coinage. Nicolaus of Damascus (b. c. 64 BC) and his father were leading Greek-speaking citizens. After c. 800 Greek lived on in Damascus only as the church language of Arabic-speaking clergy: a Greek scroll of the Liturgy of St James was copied for Damascus in the late 9th or early 10th c. (Vat. gr. 2282, with Arabic notes for the priest). From the mid-14th c. Damascus was the seat of the Orthodox patriarchs of Antioch, Arabic-speaking until 1724, with a few Greeks at their court in the 17th c. (Euthymios III of Chios, 1635-1647). From 1724 to 1898 Constantinople named Greek patriarchs, but they were often away (Sylvester for years at a time in the Danubian lands and Constantinople), and only single Greek clerics lived with them; the secretaries, the parish clergy and the people spoke Arabic. A small Greek community has existed since 1913 (about 150 members today), mostly Syrians of Greek descent. Neither is counted as a return of Greek speech.
sources: Jones, Cities of the Eastern Roman Provinces; Sartre, D'Alexandre a Zenobie; Burns, Damascus: A History (2005); British Museum 1861,1112.90; Pleiades 678106; Panchenko, Arab Orthodox Christians under the Ottomans 1516-1831 (2016); Radle, 'The Liturgy of St James in Medieval Damascus', OCP 87 (2021) 341-352; Walbiner, 'The split of the Greek Orthodox patriarchate of Antioch (1724)', Chronos 7 (2003) 9-36; Tipau, Sylvester of Antioch (2024)

site: probably al-Hafar, a village about 8 km south-east of Sadad, Homs Governorate (Sadad and Mahin have also been proposed); not at Hawwarin, which is Evaria
greek_from_text: Bishop Theodore of Danaba at the Council of Chalcedon, 451.
until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the Damascus-Homs road, 634-636. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
fade_evidence: Last known bishop: Eulogius, 553. Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636.
bilingual_evidence: a see with Greek-signing bishops (451, 458, 553)
status_evidence: See of Phoenice Libanensis under Damascus: bishop Theodore at Chalcedon 451 and in the letter of 458 to Leo I; Eulogius at Constantinople 553; Notitia Antiochena; Danova on the Tabula Peutingeriana.
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The Barrington Atlas puts 'Danova' at Hawwarin, which is Evaria, a separate see counted on its own; Danaba is placed here near al-Hafar, its most likely separate site (Wikipedia: Danaba), and the point is only regional. Pleiades 668236 ('Danova') is plotted at Hawwarin and is not used.
sources: Wikipedia: Danaba; Catholic Encyclopedia: Danaba; Devreesse 1945

other_names: Hemesa; Ḥimṣ (Arabic); Colonia Emesa (from Caracalla/Elagabalus); Hims
site: Homs city, Homs Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek epitaph of the Emesene prince C. Iulius Sampsigeramus on his tomb, AD 78/79; city coins with Greek legends from Antoninus Pius (138-161)
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah early in 636 and again after the Yarmuk; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
fade_evidence: Greek writers from Emesa: Heliodorus (Aethiopica), bishop Nemesius (c. 400), Romanos the Melodist (born c. 490). Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
ended_by: Surrendered to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah (with Khalid ibn al-Walid), 636, and reoccupied after the Yarmuk, 636/637 (al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari). Earlier taken by Khosrow II's army, 613. No named act ended Greek speech.
refounded_by: Roman colonia under Caracalla or Elagabalus (early 3rd c.)
pre_greek_note: The citadel tell has Bronze and Iron Age levels; no pre-Greek name of the town is securely attested.
bilingual_evidence: Arab dynasty (Sampsigeramus) and the cult of Elagabal; Greek city coins, inscriptions and writers (Heliodorus, Nemesius, Romanos the Melodist)
status_evidence: Strabo 16.2.10; city coins from 138-161; colonia; metropolis of Phoenice Libanensis (5th c.); Hierocles
note: Homs continues Emesa/Hemesa, the Greek and Latin form of the local name. Bilingual rather than Greek because of the Arab dynasty and the native cult; the balance is a judgment.
sources: Millar 1993, 300-309; Sartre 2001; Pleiades 668261; Wikipedia: Emesa

site: Hama city, Hama Governorate
greek_from_text: Antiochus IV (175-164 BC) renamed Hamath Epiphania; Seleucid and later Roman city coins with Greek legends show a polis; the renaming alone would not prove one
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah in 637/638; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
ended_by: Surrendered on terms to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 637/638 (al-Baladhuri). No named act ended Greek speech.
pre_greek_name: Ḥamath (Aramaic; Hebrew Bible Ḥămāt; Assyrian Amattu)
bilingual_evidence: the Aramaic name Hamath stayed in use beside Epiphania; Syriac-speaking Christians in late antiquity
status_evidence: Seleucid and Roman city coins; see of Syria Secunda (bishops from 325); Hierocles
note: No Greek settlers are attested; a renamed Aramaean royal city.
sources: Cohen 2006, 109-111; Grainger 1990; Pleiades 668182; Wikipedia: Hama

site: Huwwarin, near Sadad, Homs Governorate
greek_from_text: bishop Thomas of Euaria, 451; a suffragan of Damascus in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570)
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest of the Damascus-Homs road, 634-636. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is an estimate.
fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see, its bishops' Greek subscriptions and a few Greek inscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636. Yazid I died at Huwwarin in 683.
bilingual_evidence: a see in the Notitia Antiochena; Greek inscriptions of the district
status_evidence: Bishop of Euaria, 451; native bishop John; made a city in 573; suffragan of Damascus (Georgius Cyprius); Greek and Syriac inscriptions in its churches
note: Evaria is the modern Hawwarin, beside Mahin. The Barrington Atlas places 'Danova' (Danaba) at Hawwarin and Euareia 5 km to the north-east; the coordinates here follow the modern identification with Hawwarin.
sources: Devreesse 1945; Pleiades 161546548; Wikipedia: Huwwarin

other_names: Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix Heliopolitana (Roman); Baʿlabakk (Arabic)
site: Baalbek, Baalbek-Hermel Governorate
greek_from_text: Augustus settled veterans here as part of the colony of Berytus, 15/14 BC; Septimius Severus made Heliopolis a colony of its own (c. 193-201). Greek is attested among residents from the 1st c. AD.
until_text: Administration: Abu Ubayda took the city after the Roman defeat at Yarmuk (634, 636 or 637 in different accounts), by agreement according to most; it became a fortress (al-Qalʿa); Marwan II sacked it in 748. Speech: Greek-speaking residents left or shifted to Arabic; no evidence of a Greek-speaking community after the early 8th c. The date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800); the town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest.
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the 1st-6th c.; Constantine built a basilica and installed a bishop (Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.58); pagan cult to the 6th c. (Malalas); Hierocles (Phoenice Libanensis); Greek stayed in the caliphate's offices until 'Abd al-Malik's order of c. 700; the Melkite (Chalcedonian) Christians of Syria and Lebanon wrote Arabic by the 9th c. (Theodore Abu Qurra; the Arabic Melkite manuscripts of Mar Saba and Sinai).
ended_by: Taken by Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah after Yarmuk, 636/637 (al-Baladhuri); sacked by the Umayyad caliph Marwan II, 748.
founder: Augustus (veteran colony with Berytus); Septimius Severus (separate colony)
pre_greek_note: The Semitic name bʿlbk is first attested in the Mishnah (2nd c. AD, as a kind of garlic) and in 5th-c. Syriac; no securely identified pre-Greek name in earlier sources.
other_language: Aramaic (and Latin, the official language of the colony in the 1st-3rd c.)
bilingual_evidence: Greek dedications and epitaphs of residents beside the Latin of the colony; Aramaic-speaking population of the Bekaa and its pagan villagers in late antiquity (Theodoret; the Life of Rabbula).
status_evidence: Roman colony; Greek and Latin inscriptions; bishops; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena
note: A Roman foundation with Latin public life, a Greek-speaking element and an Aramaic-speaking population; recorded as bilingual (Greek and Aramaic).
sources: Strabo 16.2.10; Millar, The Roman Near East; Hajjar, La triade d'Héliopolis-Baalbek; Pleiades 678179

site: Yabrud, Qalamun, Rif Dimashq Governorate
greek_from_text: A bishop's see of Phoenice Libanensis by late antiquity (Notitia Antiochena, under Damascus); a Roman temple of Jupiter (Zeus) of Iabruda, later the church of Constantine and Helena; Greek inscriptions of residents from the Roman period
until_text: Passed to the Arabs with the Damascus region in 634-636. The see survived as an Arabic-speaking Melkite community; no evidence for Greek speech after the conquest. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the cult of Zeus Yabroudes; bishops of Iabruda in Melkite lists. Regional markers: flight of Roman inhabitants at the conquest and resettlement of the coast (al-Baladhuri); Greek in the registers until c. 700-707; Arabic Melkite writing by c. 800 (Theodore Abu Qurra).
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Damascus region, 634-636.
pre_greek_note: Pleiades records an Akkadian form Jabrudu; the attestation should be checked.
bilingual_evidence: An Aramaic-speaking district (Aramaic is still spoken in nearby Ma'loula); Greek dedications at the temple of Zeus Yabroudes and Greek epitaphs of residents
status_evidence: Ptolemy 5.15 (Iabruda); bishop's see of Phoenice Libanensis (Notitia Antiochena; Le Quien)
note: Civic status rests on the see; Greek is the language of its public inscriptions, Aramaic the language of the district.
sources: Ptolemy 5.15; Le Quien, Oriens Christianus II; Pleiades 678196

other_names: Qadesh (Egyptian qdš; Hittite Kinza); Laodicea Scabiosa (Tabula Peutingeriana)
site: Tell Nebi Mend, al-Qusayr District, Homs Governorate
greek_from_text: The Seleucid name Laodicea is attested from 221 BC, when Antiochus III set out from it into the Marsyas valley (Polybius 5.45.7-8), but no Hellenistic coins, inscriptions or settlers of the town are known. It is first named as a town of the region by Strabo (16.2.18, c. AD 20) and Pliny (NH 5.82, "Laodiceni ad Libanum"); its city coins with Greek legends (LAODIK. PROS LIBANO) begin under Septimius Severus.
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the conquest of the Homs region by Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah, 636/637; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The site later shrank to a village. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
ended_by: No named act: taken in Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Homs region, 636/637; the town then declined.
status_evidence: Strabo 16.2.18; Pliny NH 5.82; Ptolemy 5.15; city coins with Greek legends under Septimius Severus, Julia Domna, Caracalla and Severus Alexander; see of Phoenice Libanensis; Hierocles
note: A Seleucid foundation or renaming on the site of Qadesh; whether the kings settled Greeks or laid the city out anew is not known, so the Greek date follows the first sure evidence of a town (Strabo), as for Seleucia on the Belus. If only the city coins count, the date is c. 200.
sources: Cohen 2006, 117-120; Polybius 5.45.7-8; Strabo 16.2.18; Pleiades 668291; Wildwinds/RPC: Laodikeia ad Libanum (provincial coins, Severans only)

other_names: Sizara (Ptolemy 5.15.16); Sezer; Sinzar (Middle Persian, Shapur I's inscription); Shaizar (Arabic)
site: Shaizar, Mahardah District, Hama Governorate
greek_from_text: Seleucid foundation settled by colonists from Thessalian Larissa, who served in the first cavalry agema at Apamea (Diodorus 33.4a); c. 300 BC
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the surrender to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's army in 637/638; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The Roman garrison that held Shaizar from Basil II's conquest in 999 to the Banu Munqidh in 1081 does not count as a resident community. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
ended_by: Surrendered to Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's army, 637/638 (al-Baladhuri). No named act ended Greek speech.
pre_greek_note: Sinzar/Zinzar of the Amarna letters and the Egyptian lists is usually identified with Shaizar, but not certainly.
status_evidence: Appian Syr. 57; Diodorus 33.4a; Strabo 16.2.10; see of Syria Secunda; Hierocles
note: Its Thessalian settlers are among the few attested Greek colonists in Seleucid Syria.
sources: Cohen 2006, 116-118; Diodorus 33.4a; Pleiades 668292; Wikipedia: Shaizar

site: Maryamin, northwest of Homs, Homs Governorate
greek_from_text: A see of Syria Secunda in the council lists and Hierocles, from about the 5th c.; the native town is attested from 333 BC (Arrian 2.13.8).
until_text: Administration: taken in Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Orontes valley, 637/638. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is the estimate for Syriac-majority towns, c. 640 (636-750).
fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see and its bishops' Greek subscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
ended_by: No named act: taken in Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Orontes valley, 637/638.
pre_greek_note: Hecataeus (in Stephanus) calls it a Phoenician city; Arrian (2.13.8) names Mariamme among the towns that surrendered to Parmenion in 333 BC; no non-Greek attestation of the name.
bilingual_evidence: A Phoenician town of the Aradian hinterland (Arrian 2.13.8); in Roman times a see whose bishops signed in Greek, in an Aramaic-speaking district.
status_evidence: See of Syria II under Apamea (council lists; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena).
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The mosaic of women musicians (late 4th c.) is the town's best-known find. Located at Maryamin after the Barrington Atlas; some place it at Qal'at al-Hosn.
sources: Jones 1971; Arrian 2.13.8; Pleiades 668308; Wikipedia: Mariamme

other_names: Tadmor (Palmyrene Aramaic Tdmr; Akkadian Tadmar; Hebrew Bible); Hadriana Palmyra (Hadrian); Tadmur (Arabic)
site: Palmyra ruins beside the town of Tadmur, Homs Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek-Palmyrene bilingual inscriptions of residents from the 1st c. AD, after the city came under Roman control (Tiberius); boule and demos attested in the later 1st c.
until_text: Administration: the city surrendered to Khalid ibn al-Walid in 634. Speech: Palmyrene Aramaic disappears from inscriptions after 272-274; Greek inscriptions continue, fewer, until 562 (IGLS XVII). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
fade_evidence: Over 500 Greek inscriptions; the last dated Greek inscription is of 562; bishops from 325 (Marinus at Nicaea).
ended_by: Surrendered to Khalid ibn al-Walid on his desert march, 634 (al-Baladhuri, al-Tabari). Earlier sacked by Aurelian after its second revolt, 273; Marwan II razed its walls, 745.
refounded_by: Hadrian (Hadriana Palmyra, 129); colonia in the early 3rd c.; Diocletian's camp; Justinian (walls)
pre_greek_name: Tadmar (Akkadian, Mari and Assyrian texts); Tadmor (Hebrew Bible); Tdmr (Palmyrene Aramaic)
bilingual_evidence: hundreds of Greek-Palmyrene bilingual inscriptions, the bilingual Tariff of 137; boule and demos in Greek; Palmyrene Aramaic the first language of most citizens
status_evidence: boule and demos in bilingual inscriptions; Tariff of 137; Roman colonia; see (Marinus at Nicaea 325); Hierocles
sources: IGLS XVII.1; Millar 1993, 319-336; Yon 2002; Pleiades 668331; Wikipedia: Palmyrene inscriptions

other_names: Raphanea; Rephania (Middle Persian, Shapur I's inscription); Rafaniya (Arabic)
site: Rafniyah, Masyaf District, Hama Governorate
greek_from_text: 1st c. AD: the Raphanaei in Pliny (NH 5.82) and Raphanea in Josephus (BJ 7.97), beside the legionary fortress; city coins with Greek legends under Elagabalus
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Orontes valley, 637/638; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
ended_by: No named act: taken in Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Orontes valley, 637/638; earlier taken by Shapur I, c. 253 (Shapur I's inscription).
status_evidence: Josephus BJ 7.97; base of legio III Gallica; city coins under Elagabalus; see of Syria Secunda (bishops from 325, Bassianus at Nicaea, to 536); Hierocles; Georgius Cyprius
note: The town grew beside a Roman legionary fortress; the Greek-speaking civilian community is inferred from its coins and see.
sources: Jones 1971; Josephus, BJ 7.97; Pleiades 668350; Wikipedia: Raphanea

site: Salamiyah, Salamiyah District, Hama Governorate
greek_from_text: bishop Julian of Salamias at the consecration of Severus of Antioch, 512
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 636. Speech: the small Greek-speaking element (clergy, notables) is not attested after the conquest; the Aramaic-speaking Christians who stayed turned to Arabic. The date is an estimate.
fade_evidence: Greek here is known mainly from the see, its bishops' Greek subscriptions and a few Greek inscriptions; the townspeople mostly spoke Aramaic (Syriac). No Greek-speaking community is attested after the conquest.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the Homs region, 636.
bilingual_evidence: a see by 512 and Greek inscriptions (temple of Zeus, later a church); an Aramaic-speaking district
status_evidence: Bishop Julian at the consecration of Severus of Antioch, 512; church inscriptions of the 6th-7th c. (a church of the Theotokos dated 604)
note: Its province is uncertain (Phoenice Libanensis or Syria Secunda). The Greek date is the first sure one; Greek may be older.
sources: Devreesse 1945; Pleiades 668362; Wikipedia: Salamiyah

other_names: Seleucobelus (late Roman); Seleucenses ad Belum (Pliny NH 5.82)
site: probably near Jisr al-Shughur, Idlib Governorate (Pleiades); al-Suqaylabiyah, Hama Governorate, has also been proposed
greek_from_text: First named as a town of Syria by Pliny (NH 5.82, AD 77) and Ptolemy; later the see of Seleucobelus in Syria Secunda. The dynastic name shows a Seleucid settlement, but no Hellenistic polis is attested.
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of the Orontes valley, 637/638; Greek remained in the tax offices until c. 700. Speech: part of the Greek-speaking elite left with the Roman army; the Christians who stayed spoke Aramaic and turned to Arabic. The town has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for inner Syria and Phoenicia, c. 700 (640-800).
fade_evidence: Greek stayed in the caliphal tax offices until the switch to Arabic c. 700 (Abd al-Malik, al-Walid I); by the 9th c. the Melkites of Syria wrote in Arabic (Theodore Abu Qurra); no later Greek-speaking community is attested here.
ended_by: No named act: taken in Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah's conquest of northern Syria, 637/638.
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.82; Ptolemy; see of Syria Secunda (Seleucobelus); Hierocles
note: The dynastic name shows a Seleucid settlement, but a city is attested only from Pliny and the later see. The site is not securely located: Pleiades and Cohen point to the Jisr al-Shughur area; others place it at al-Suqaylabiyah in the Ghab (Hama Governorate), whose name is usually derived from Seleucobelus.
sources: Cohen 2006, 138-139; Pliny NH 5.82; Pleiades 668364

site: Tell Blakhiyah (Anthedon Harbour), north-west of Gaza City, Gaza Governorate
greek_from_text: Hellenistic town with a Greek name; taken by Alexander Jannaeus c. 100 BC (Josephus AJ 13.357) and rebuilt by Gabinius (BJ 1.166); Herod renamed it Agrippias
until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the Gaza coast, 634-637. Speech: no later Greek-speaking community is attested; the site was later abandoned. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Late Roman harbour town; bishops of Anthedon to the 6th c. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken with Gaza by the army of Amr ibn al-As, 634-637
status_evidence: Josephus AJ 13.357, BJ 1.166, AJ 15.217; see of Palaestina I (Hierocles)
note: Coordinates are for the excavated harbour town at Blakhiyah; the Pleiades point lies about 3 km inland. The Greek name may point to Greek settlers, but this is not attested.
sources: Josephus BJ 1.166, 1.416; Humbert et al., Blakhiyah excavations; Pleiades 687826; Wikipedia: Anthedon Harbour

other_names: Pegai (Hellenistic); Ras al-'Ayn (Arabic); Migdal Afek / Mirabel (later fort)
site: Tel Afek (Ras el-Ein) in the Yarkon National Park (Mekorot HaYarkon), between Rosh HaAyin and Petah Tikva, Central District
greek_from_text: Herod founded Antipatris for his father Antipater, c. 9 BC (Josephus AJ 16.142-143), on the site of Hellenistic Pegai
until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636. Speech: the town had declined after the earthquake of 363; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: City coins under Elagabalus with Greek legends; bishops of Antipatris to the 6th c. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636
pre_greek_name: ʾĂp̄ēq (Hebrew Bible); Apqu (Akkadian, Esarhaddon); ʾIpq (Egyptian, Thutmose III)
status_evidence: Josephus AJ 16.142-143; city coins (Elagabalus); see of Palaestina I
sources: Josephus AJ 16.142-143; Kochavi, Aphek-Antipatris; Pleiades 687996; Wikipedia: Antipatris

site: Tel Arsuf (Apollonia National Park), Herzliya, Tel Aviv District
greek_from_text: Hellenistic town with the Greek name Apollonia; held by Alexander Jannaeus and rebuilt by Gabinius (Josephus AJ 13.395; BJ 1.166)
until_text: Administration: taken with the other coastal towns in the Arab conquest, c. 640. Speech: Arsuf became a Muslim coastal stronghold; no later Greek-speaking community is attested. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Late Roman town with churches and Greek inscriptions (Sozusa); Samaritan presence; Umayyad and Abbasid fortified town. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: Taken by Mu'awiya's forces with the other coastal towns, c. 640 (Baladhuri)
pre_greek_note: The Arabic Arsuf is often derived from the Phoenician god Reshef, but no non-Greek name of the town is attested.
status_evidence: Josephus BJ 1.166; Pliny 5.69; Ptolemy 5.16.2; Hierocles (Sozusa); see of Palaestina I, with bishops in 449, 518 and 553
note: The Greek date rests on the name and on Josephus; the excavations show a Hellenistic town over a Persian-period Phoenician settlement. The ruins lie in the Apollonia National Park at the northern edge of Herzliya; the site is also known by its medieval name, Arsuf.
sources: Josephus BJ 1.166; Roll and Ayalon, Apollonia and Southern Sharon; Pleiades 678025; Wikipedia: Apollonia-Arsuf

site: Khirbat al-Beiyudat, Jordan valley north of Jericho, Jericho Governorate
greek_from_text: Founded by the ethnarch Archelaus c. AD 6 for the workers of his date groves (Josephus AJ 17.340); first attested as a see with bishop Timotheus at the synods of Constantinople, 448 and 449, and Antiochus at Chalcedon, 451
until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the 630s. Speech: no later Greek-speaking community is attested; the site was later abandoned. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Church mosaic with Greek inscriptions of the 560s. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the 630s
status_evidence: Josephus AJ 17.340; Pliny 13.44 (its dates); bishops 448, 449 and 451; Madaba map; dated church mosaic inscriptions of the 560s at Khirbet el-Beiyudat
note: A village-town that became a see; the Greek of its church is attested, but the speech of its early, probably Jewish, plantation workers is not, so it is dated only from the see.
sources: Josephus AJ 17.340; Wikipedia: Archelais; Pleiades 687831

site: Tel Ashkelon National Park, Ashkelon, Southern District
greek_from_text: Hellenistic Greek city: Ascalonites in Greek inscriptions at Delos and Athens in the 2nd c. BC; its own era of freedom from 104 BC; the philosophers Antiochus and Aristus of Ascalon
until_text: Administration: Mu'awiya took the city c. 640-644. Speech: Baladhuri says Roman forces later raided it and removed its people, and 'Abd al-Malik rebuilt and garrisoned it; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c.
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and bishops to the 6th c.; Baladhuri on the Roman raid and the Umayyad resettlement
ended_by: Taken by Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, c. 640-644; later emptied in a Roman raid and resettled by 'Abd al-Malik (Baladhuri)
pre_greek_name: ʾAšqəlōn (Hebrew Bible); Ashkelon (Egyptian, Merneptah stele); Asqaluna (Akkadian)
status_evidence: Free city with its own era (104 BC) and Greek civic coins; Greek writers; see of Palaestina I (Longinus at Nicaea 325)
note: Greek pottery in the city sacked by Nebuchadnezzar in 604 BC is evidence of trade, not of a Greek city. Its harbour, Maiumas of Ascalon, is noted as a close call.
sources: Strabo 16.2.29; Fuks, Ascalon in the Hellenistic and Roman periods; Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; Pleiades 687839; Wikipedia: Ashkelon

other_names: Azotus Mesogaios, Azotus Hippenos (late Roman); Ashdod (Hebrew Bible); Isdud (Arabic)
site: Tel Ashdod by the former village of Isdud, Ashdod, Southern District
greek_from_text: Hellenistic town: Jonathan burned Azotus and its temple of Dagon in 147 BC (1 Macc 10:84); Pompey restored it to its citizens and Gabinius rebuilt it (Josephus AJ 14.75, 14.88)
until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the 630s. Speech: Isdud became a village; no later Greek-speaking community is attested. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishops of Azotus to the 6th c.; the Madaba map shows Azotus and Azotus Paralios. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of Palaestina, 634-640; Jonathan the Hasmonaean had burned the town, 147 BC (1 Macc 10:84)
status_evidence: Josephus AJ 14.75, 14.88; Pliny 5.68; Hierocles (Azotus Mesogaios); see of Palaestina I (Silvanus at Nicaea 325)
note: The gap 147-57 BC follows Jonathan's destruction and Hasmonaean rule. Acts 8:40 places Philip the evangelist here. Tel Ashdod is a ruin a few kilometres south-east of the modern city of Ashdod (founded 1956), which takes the ancient name; the Arab village of Isdud on the site, which continued the name, was depopulated in 1948.
sources: 1 Macc 10:84; Josephus AJ 14.88; Dothan, Ashdod excavation reports; Pleiades 687838; Wikipedia: Ashdod

site: Ashdod-Yam (Minat el-Qal'a), Ashdod, Southern District
greek_from_text: The harbour town of Azotus became a city of its own in late antiquity: Azotus Paralios in Hierocles (c. 527) and on the Madaba map
until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of the 630s. Speech: the site later became a Muslim coastal fort (Minat al-Qal'a); no later Greek-speaking community is attested. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Late Roman town with Greek inscriptions; Islamic-period fort on the shore. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of the coast, 630s-640s
pre_greek_note: Asdūdimmu is usually taken as Ashdod's harbour; its identification with this site is probable, not certain.
status_evidence: Hierocles (Azotus Paralios); Madaba map; see of Palaestina I
note: Earlier part of the polis of Azotus; counted from when it is listed as a city in its own right.
sources: Hierocles, Synecdemus (Palaestina I); Madaba map; Pleiades 687843; Wikipedia: Ashdod-Yam

site: el-Araj (Beit HaBek) on the north shore of the Sea of Galilee, or et-Tell c. 2 km inland to the north-north-east; both east of the Jordan mouth, Golan Heights
admin1: Golan Heights (Syrian territory occupied by Israel since 1967)
greek_from_text: Philip the Tetrarch raised the village of Bethsaida to a polis and named it Julias (Josephus AJ 18.28); dated before 2 BC (after Augustus' daughter) or c. AD 30 (after Livia-Julia)
until_text: The town suffered in the Jewish War; at et-Tell the Roman settlement shrank after 67/68 and the site was abandoned by the 3rd-4th century. Evidence for Greek speech is thin throughout.
fade_evidence: Josephus, Vita 398-406 (fighting near Julias, AD 67); excavations at et-Tell (Arav) and el-Araj (Notley, Aviam)
ended_by: No named act: fighting near Julias in the Jewish War (Josephus, Vita 398-406, AD 67); the town then declined.
bilingual_evidence: A Jewish fishing town raised to a polis by Philip; the apostles Philip and Andrew from Bethsaida bore Greek names, and 'Greeks' approached Philip there (John 12:20-21)
status_evidence: Josephus AJ 18.28 and BJ 2.168 (polis named Julias); Pliny NH 5.71
note: The location is disputed between et-Tell (excavated since 1987) and el-Araj on the shore, where recent excavations found a Roman-period settlement; the point is at el-Araj. Greek speech by residents is inferred, not directly attested.
sources: Josephus AJ 18.28; Arav and Freund (eds.), Bethsaida I-IV; Schurer-Vermes-Millar II, 171-172; Pleiades 678065

other_names: Straton's Tower (Στράτωνος Πύργος, Hellenistic); Caesarea Sebaste; Kaisareia Paralios; Colonia Prima Flavia Augusta Caesarensis (Vespasian); Qaysariyya (Arabic)
site: Caesarea National Park and the town of Caesarea, Haifa District
greek_from_text: Straton's Tower, a Hellenistic port town (Zenon papyri, 259 BC), was taken by Alexander Jannaeus c. 100 BC and restored to its citizens as a free city by Pompey in 63 BC (Josephus AJ 14.76); Herod refounded it as Caesarea, 22-10/9 BC
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended when Mu'awiya took the city in 640/641 after a long siege. Speech: the Greek-speaking élite left by sea or was taken captive; the shrunken Arab town of Qaysariyya is not known to have kept a Greek-speaking community.
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and writers to the 6th c. (Procopius of Caesarea); the conquest of 640/641 with captives sent to the caliph (Baladhuri)
ended_by: Taken by Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan after a long siege, 640/641; Baladhuri reports thousands of captives sent to the caliph Umar
refounded_by: Herod (as Caesarea, with a new city and harbour, 22-10/9 BC); Vespasian (Roman colonia, after 70)
pre_greek_note: Straton's Tower is a Greek name, probably after a Sidonian king Straton (Abdashtart); no non-Greek name of the town is attested.
status_evidence: Herodian foundation (Josephus AJ 15.331-341); Roman colonia; capital of Judaea and metropolis of Palaestina I; bishops from the 2nd c. (Eusebius); writers Eusebius and Procopius
note: Jewish and Samaritan communities lived beside the Greek-speaking majority; the clash between Jews and Greeks here in AD 66 began the Jewish revolt. Counted as a Hellenized native town: Straton's Tower was already a free Greek city in 63 BC, and Herod rebuilt it as Caesarea on the same site.
sources: Josephus AJ 15.331-341; Holum et al., King Herod's Dream (1988); Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan; Pleiades 678401; Wikipedia: Caesarea Maritima

site: Beit Ras, Irbid Governorate
greek_from_text: Founded in 97/98, the start of the city's era, under Nerva or Trajan
until_text: Taken by the Arabs in 635-636. Christian Greek speakers remained under the Umayyads: Peter of Capitolias, a local priest, was executed in 715. The town declined after the earthquake of 749. other_names: Seleucia (Seleucid name on coins, 2nd c. BC); ʿAzzah (Hebrew Bible); Ghazza (Arabic)
site: Tell Harube and the old city of Gaza, Gaza Governorate
greek_from_text: Hellenistic Greek city: Polybius praises its loyalty when Antiochus III besieged it, 201 BC (16.22a); city coins as Seleucia in the 2nd c. BC. Alexander had taken it in 332 BC and resettled it with people from the neighbourhood (Arrian 2.27)
until_text: Administration: the Roman army was defeated at Dathin in 634 and Gaza was taken by Amr ibn al-As c. 637. Speech: the Greek-speaking Christian community survived the conquest but, like the rest of the Palestinian Melkites, shifted to Arabic in the 8th-9th c.
fade_evidence: The rhetorical school of Gaza (Aeneas, Procopius, Choricius) to the mid-6th c.; Greek church inscriptions into the 7th c.; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: Taken by Amr ibn al-As, c. 637, after the battle of Dathin (634); the Roman garrison was put to death in 638/639 (Passion of the Sixty Martyrs of Gaza). No named act ended Greek speech. Earlier, Alexander Jannaeus destroyed the city c. 96 BC (Josephus AJ 13.358-364)
pre_greek_name: ʿAzzāh (Hebrew Bible); Ḫazzatu (Akkadian); Gḏt (Egyptian, Thutmose III)
status_evidence: Greek civic coins (Hellenistic and Roman, era of 61 BC); rebuilt by Gabinius; Greek writers of the school of Gaza; see of Palaestina I (Asclepas at Nicaea 325)
note: The gap 96-57 BC follows Jannaeus' massacre and destruction. The countryside spoke Aramaic and the city had Arab traders; the 'Minoa' legend is a legend. Its port, Maiumas-Constantia, is a separate entry.
sources: Arrian 2.26-27; Josephus AJ 13.358-364; Glucker, The City of Gaza (1987); Pleiades 687902; Wikipedia: Gaza City

other_names: Antiochia in Jerusalem (Seleucid polis, 175-164 BC); Colonia Aelia Capitolina (Hadrian); Yerushalayim (Hebrew); al-Quds, Bayt al-Maqdis, Iliya' (Arabic)
site: The Old City of Jerusalem
greek_from_text: The high priest Jason made Jerusalem the polis of 'Antiochenes in Jerusalem', with a gymnasium and ephebes, under Antiochus IV, 175 BC (2 Macc 4:9-12)
until_text: No end: Greek speakers have lived in Jerusalem without a long break from 175 BC to today. From the 9th c., when the Orthodox laity turned to Arabic, Greek was kept by the clergy and monks of the Holy Sepulchre and the patriarchate: the survey of c. 808 found Greek dominant among them; the service book of the Holy Sepulchre was copied in Greek in 1122; pilgrims saw Greek monks holding the choir and singing the office in Greek (Adorno, 1470-71); and the Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre, Greek by rule, has led the patriarchate since the 1530s. Lay Greeks settled again from the mid-19th c.
until_basis: continuous: clergy and monks; lay Greeks again from the 19th c.
fade_evidence: Continuity: a Greek loan contract written in Jerusalem, 115 (P.Mur. 114), and Hadrian's Greek letter from Jerusalem, 130; Egeria 47 (c. 384: the bishop preaches in Greek); the Commemoratorium (c. 808: 150 clergy and staff at the Holy Sepulchre under a synkellos; 11 hermits on the Mount of Olives singing the psalms in Greek, one in Arabic); Michael Synkellos and the Graptoi brothers writing Greek in the city (811-813); the synkellos Elias at Constantinople (869); Nasir-i Khusraw (1047); the Anastasis Typikon (Hagios Stavros gr. 43, copied 1122 by a lector of the Holy Sepulchre, with the homily translated into Arabic for those who could not read Greek); Daniel the Abbot (1106/07: the Orthodox priests over the Holy Sepulchre); the Greek homilies of Patriarch Athanasios II (1230s); the Greek decree of the synod of 1443; Adorno (1470-71) and Casola (1494) on the Greek monks and altars of the Holy Sepulchre; Fernberger (1592); Horn (c. 1740); the census of 1922 (c. 700-760 Greek speakers in Jerusalem); today the Brotherhood of the Holy Sepulchre (c. 100-120 monks, almost all Greeks and Cypriots), the Patriarchal School of Sion and the Greek Consulate General (since 1862).
ended_by: No end. Short interruptions: the Persian sack of 614 (clergy killed or deported; Modestus restored the churches within a few years); al-Hakim's destruction of the Holy Sepulchre, 1009 (the patriarch in hiding to 1013; rebuilt by 1048); the Latin takeover of the Holy Sepulchre, 1099 (the Greek priests back at the tomb by 1106/07; the patriarchs in exile to c. 1204); the Khwarazmian sack of 1244.
pre_greek_name: Urusalim (Akkadian, Amarna letters); Rušalimum (Egyptian execration texts); Yərūšālayim (Hebrew Bible)
other_language: Hebrew and Aramaic (Jewish), to 70; Christian Palestinian Aramaic in late antiquity; Arabic, the language of the Orthodox laity from the 9th c.
bilingual_evidence: Gymnasium, ephebes and the polis of 'Antiochenes in Jerusalem', 175 BC (2 Macc 4:9-12); Greek-speaking Jews of the Second Temple (the Theodotos synagogue inscription; about a third of ossuary inscriptions in Greek; the 'Hellenists' of Acts 6:1); in Aelia, Egeria (c. 384) heard the bishop preach in Greek with translation into Aramaic and Latin
status_evidence: 2 Macc 4:9-12; Roman colonia; Hierocles (Aelia); bishopric, patriarchate from 451
note: 70-135: the city was the base of the Tenth Legion; Greek is attested there (P.Mur. 114, 115; Hadrian's letter, 130), though no civic or church community is. From the 9th c. the Greek speakers were the clergy and monks and, from the mid-19th c., a lay community again. The Greek clergy and monks count as a resident Greek-speaking community, with no long break; Greek used only in the liturgy by Arabic speakers would not. The Seleucid citadel (Akra) kept a Greek garrison until 141 BC. Before 175 BC: from Alexander (332 BC) Jerusalem was a Jewish temple city under its high priest, and its only Greek speakers were officials and the Ptolemaic garrison in the citadel, which Antiochus III drove out c. 200 BC (Josephus, AJ 12.133-138); garrisons do not count, so the record starts with Jason's polis of 175 BC.
sources: 2 Macc 4:9-12; Egeria, Itinerarium 47; Hengel, The 'Hellenization' of Judaea (1989); Pleiades 687928; Wikipedia: Aelia Capitolina; McCormick, Charlemagne's Survey of the Holy Land (2011); Galadza, 'Greek liturgy in crusader Jerusalem', JMH 43 (2017) 421-437; Pahlitzsch, Graeci und Suriani im Palastina der Kreuzfahrerzeit (2001); Saletti, 'Ululant more luporum', Annali online Ferrara (Adorno, 1470-71); Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 12.133-138; Bertram and Luke, Report... on the Orthodox Patriarchate of Jerusalem (1921); Papastathis, 'The Greek Community of Jerusalem' (2021); Eck, Electrum 26 (2019) 129-139

Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 634-636.
founder: Herod Antipas (walls and the name Julias/Livias, c. AD 20; no Greek settlers known)
bilingual_evidence: A Jewish town of Peraea refounded by Herod Antipas; a see of the Greek-speaking church from the 4th c.; the Greek and Aramaic documents of the Babatha archive show both languages in the region.
status_evidence: See of Palaestina I: bishops Letoius at Ephesus 431, Pancratius at Chalcedon 451 and Zacharias at the synod of Jerusalem 536 (Le Quien); Hierocles (Palaestina I); Josephus AJ 18.27 and BJ 2.168 for Herod Antipas' town; Ptolemy 5.16.
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The see alone now carries it; the Herodian dynastic name is not counted as evidence, so the date is that of the first bishop.
sources: Josephus AJ 18.27; Schurer-Vermes-Millar II, 176-178; Catholic Encyclopedia: Livias (after Le Quien III 655); Pleiades 697697

other_names: Lod (Hebrew); Diospolis (Septimius Severus, 199/200); Georgioupolis (late, after St George); al-Ludd (Arabic)
site: Lod, Central District
greek_from_text: Septimius Severus made Lydda the city of Diospolis, AD 199/200 (city era and coins)
until_text: Administration: surrendered to Amr ibn al-As, c. 636, and was the first seat of the Arab district of Filastin. Speech: the caliph Sulayman moved the capital and much of the population to his new town of Ramla, c. 715; the Christians of Ludd later spoke Arabic.
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and bishops to the 6th c.; the synod of Diospolis (415); Ramla founded c. 715 (Baladhuri)
ended_by: No named act: surrendered to Amr ibn al-As, c. 636; Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik moved its people to Ramla, c. 715 (Baladhuri)
bilingual_evidence: Greek city coins of Diospolis (Septimius Severus); Greek inscriptions and bishops; a rabbinic centre in the 2nd-4th c.; Samaritans in late antiquity
status_evidence: Greek city coins; see of Palaestina I (Aetius at Nicaea 325); synod of 415
note: Before 200 Lydda was a Jewish toparchy capital, burned by Cestius Gallus in 66; the Greek city dates from Septimius Severus.
sources: Josephus BJ 2.515-516; Schwartz, Lod (Lydda), Israel (1991); Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan (Ramla); Pleiades 687953; Wikipedia: Lod

other_names: Gazaion Limen, 'harbour of the Gazaeans' (Greek); Constantia (Constantine, c. 331); Neapolis (late Roman)
site: The shore of Gaza City (al-Shati and al-Rimal area), Gaza Governorate
greek_from_text: Constantine made the port of Gaza a separate city named Constantia after its people turned Christian, c. 331 (Eusebius, Life of Constantine 4.38; Sozomen 5.3)
until_text: Administration: taken with Gaza in the Arab conquest, c. 637. Speech: no later Greek-speaking community is attested. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishops of Maiumas to the 6th c.; the synagogue of Gaza-Maiumas (508/509) with Greek dedications. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken with Gaza by Amr ibn al-As, c. 637
refounded_by: Julian put it back under Gaza (362); its separate see survived (Sozomen 5.3)
status_evidence: Eusebius VC 4.38; Sozomen 5.3; see of Palaestina I; Hierocles
note: Earlier the harbour of the Greek city of Gaza. The Jewish synagogue here (508/509) had Greek inscriptions.
sources: Eusebius, Vita Constantini 4.38; Sozomen, HE 5.3; Pleiades 687903; Wikipedia: Maiuma

site: Tel Maresha, Beit Guvrin-Maresha National Park, Southern District
greek_from_text: Sidonian community writing Greek in the painted tombs, 3rd c. BC; Marisa appears in the Zenon papyri, 259 BC
until_text: Administration and speech ended together: the Parthians destroyed the city in 40 BC and it was not rebuilt; Beth Guvrin nearby took its place.
fade_evidence: Destruction layer of 40 BC; no later occupation of the city
ended_by: Destroyed by the Parthians in 40 BC, during their invasion in support of Antigonus (Josephus AJ 14.364; BJ 1.269). Earlier conquered by John Hyrcanus, c. 112 BC (AJ 13.257)
other_language: Aramaic (Idumaean); Phoenician names among the Sidonian settlers
bilingual_evidence: Greek painted inscriptions in the tombs of the Sidonian community (Apollophanes, 'chief of the Sidonians in Marisa', 3rd-2nd c. BC); Greek graffiti, curse tablets and ostraca beside Aramaic ostraca of Idumaean residents
status_evidence: Polis freed by Pompey and rebuilt by Gabinius; Sidonian community (tomb inscriptions); Zenon papyri
note: Idumaean town; 'Aramaean town' is used for its Aramaic-speaking Idumaean base.
sources: Josephus AJ 13.257; 14.364; Peters and Thiersch, Painted Tombs of Marissa (1905); Kloner, Maresha excavations; Pleiades 687966; Wikipedia: Tel Maresha

other_names: Castrum Moenoenum (Notitia Dignitatum, fort); Ma'on (Hebrew); Khirbat al-Ma'in (Arabic)
site: Horvat Ma'on (Khirbat al-Ma'in), near Nirim, Southern District
greek_from_text: 'A little town near Gaza' (Eusebius, Onomasticon); first attested as a see with bishop Zosimus at Ephesus (449) and Chalcedon (451).
until_text: Administration: taken with the Gaza district in 'Amr ibn al-'As's conquest, 634-637. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Last bishop known: at the synod of Jerusalem, 536. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken with the Gaza district in the Arab conquest, 634-637
other_language: Aramaic (also Jewish Aramaic: the synagogue mosaic)
bilingual_evidence: A see whose bishops sat at the councils of 449, 451, 518 and 536; a Jewish community with an Aramaic synagogue inscription; Greek church mosaics in the neighbouring village of Kissufim (576).
status_evidence: See of Palaestina I: bishop Zosimus at Ephesus 449 and Chalcedon 451; bishops at the synods of Jerusalem 518 and 536 (Le Quien). Later the fort Castrum Moenoenum (Notitia Dignitatum).
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The one inscription from the site itself is the Aramaic dedication of its synagogue mosaic; the Greek church mosaics of the area are at Kissufim.
sources: Eusebius, Onomasticon; Le Quien, Oriens Christianus III; TIR Iudaea-Palaestina (1994); Pleiades 687964

other_names: Flavia Neapolis (Vespasian); Colonia Iulia Sergia Neapolis (Philip, 244); Nablus (Arabic); Shekhem (modern Hebrew usage)
site: Nablus, Nablus Governorate
greek_from_text: Vespasian founded Flavia Neapolis beside the Samaritan village of Mabartha, AD 72/73 (Josephus BJ 4.449; city era of 72/73)
until_text: Administration: surrendered on terms to Amr ibn al-As, c. 636. Speech: Greek-speaking Christians remained for a time; Samaritans and Christians later spoke Arabic. No Greek-speaking community is attested after the 8th c.
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions to the 6th c.; the Samaritan revolts of 484 and 529, crushed by Zeno and Justinian, cut the Samaritan population
ended_by: No named act: surrendered on terms to Amr ibn al-As, c. 636
pre_greek_note: Mabartha/Mamortha is known only from Josephus and Pliny. Biblical Shechem lies at Tell Balata, about 1.5 km east, and is a separate site.
bilingual_evidence: Greek civic coinage from AD 72/73; Justin Martyr, a native who wrote in Greek (2nd c.); Greek inscriptions; the city was the centre of the Samaritans, who spoke Aramaic
status_evidence: Josephus BJ 4.449; Greek city coins; Roman colonia; see of Palaestina I (Germanus at Nicaea 325)
sources: Josephus BJ 4.449; Pliny 5.69; Magen, Flavia Neapolis (2005); Pleiades 678301; Wikipedia: Nablus

site: Tabaqat Fahl, North Jordan Valley, Irbid Governorate
greek_from_text: Taken by Antiochus III in 218 BC (Polybius 5.70); the Macedonian name was given to the native town of Pihil, probably in the 3rd century BC
until_text: Destroyed by Alexander Jannaeus c. 83 BC because the townspeople would not adopt Jewish customs (Josephus AJ 13.397); restored by Pompey. The Arabs defeated the Roman army at Fahl in 635; the Umayyad town was destroyed by the earthquake of 749. A smaller town went on after the earthquake. Pella has no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest, so the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the West and East churches; Umayyad houses destroyed in the earthquake of 18 January 749. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: Destroyed by Alexander Jannaeus, c. 83 BC; restored by Pompey, 63 BC. Battle of Fahl, January 635 (Abu Ubayda, Khalid ibn al-Walid, Shurahbil ibn Hasana); the earthquake of 749 ruined the town.
pre_greek_name: Pḥl (Egyptian execration texts and lists); Piḫilu (Akkadian, Amarna letters)
status_evidence: Polybius 5.70; Josephus AJ 13.397; Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); city coins; bishops; Hierocles (Palaestina II)
note: The Greek name was later linked to Alexander's Pella; no Macedonian settlers are attested.
sources: Polybius 5.70; Smith and McNicoll, Pella in Jordan; Schurer-Vermes-Millar II, 145-148; Pleiades 678326

site: Tel Bet Yerah (Khirbat al-Karak), south-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, Northern District
greek_from_text: Ptolemaic foundation named for Philotera, sister of Ptolemy II; Antiochus III took it in 218 BC (Polybius 5.70.3-4)
until_text: Administration and speech ended together: the Hasmonaeans took the town, and the Hellenistic settlement on the tell was abandoned in the early 1st c. BC.
fade_evidence: Hellenistic houses and coins to the late 2nd c. BC; no later Greek town
ended_by: Taken by Alexander Jannaeus, c. 100-80 BC (Syncellus lists Philoteria among his conquests)
pre_greek_note: The tell holds a large Bronze Age town whose ancient name is not attested; Beth Yerah is a later rabbinic name.
status_evidence: Polybius 5.70.3-4; Cohen 2006 (Philoteria)
note: The identification with Tel Bet Yerah is generally accepted but not proven.
sources: Polybius 5.70.3-4; Cohen 2006 (Philoteria); Pleiades 678333; Wikipedia: Tel Bet Yerah

site: Tell Rafah, Rafah, Rafah Governorate (on the line between the Gaza Strip and Egypt)
greek_from_text: Hellenistic town, 'the first city of Coele Syria towards Egypt' (Polybius 5.80), by which Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III in 217 BC; taken by Alexander Jannaeus and rebuilt by Gabinius (Josephus AJ 13.357; BJ 1.166)
until_text: Administration: on the route of the Arab invasion of 633/634, taken with the rest of the Gaza district. Speech: no later Greek-speaking community is attested. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Roman city coins with Greek legends (2nd-3rd c.); bishops of Raphia to the 6th c. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken by the army of Amr ibn al-As in the invasion of 633/634
pre_greek_name: Rapiḫu (Akkadian, Sargon II); Rph (Egyptian, Seti I)
status_evidence: Polybius 5.80-86; Josephus BJ 1.166; Roman city coins dated by an era of 57 BC (Gabinius); see of Palaestina I (5th-6th c.)
note: Tell Rafah lies on or very near the line between the Gaza Strip and Egypt; the main ruins are counted to the Gaza Strip here, as the set's area rules say.
sources: Polybius 5.80-86; Josephus AJ 13.357; Pleiades 688015; Wikipedia: Rafah

other_names: Nysa (Hellenistic dynastic name); Bet She'an (Hebrew); Baysan (Arabic)
site: Tel Beit She'an and Beit She'an National Park, Northern District
greek_from_text: A Greek city by 218 BC, when Antiochus III took it (Polybius 5.70.4); probably a Ptolemaic foundation of the 3rd c. BC, also called Nysa
until_text: Administration: surrendered to the Arab armies after the battle of Fahl (Pella), 635. Speech: Greek-speaking Christians remained; the Umayyad market inscription of Hisham's reign (c. 737/738) is in Arabic, and the earthquake of 749 ruined the city centre, after which Baysan was a small Arabic-speaking town.
fade_evidence: Greek building inscriptions into the 7th c.; Cyril of Scythopolis (6th c.); Arabic market inscription of Hisham (c. 737/738); earthquake of 18 January 749
ended_by: No named act: surrendered after the battle of Fahl, 635; the earthquake of 749 destroyed the city. Earlier the sons of John Hyrcanus took it, c. 107 BC, and its people went into exile (Josephus AJ 13.280; Megillat Ta'anit)
pre_greek_name: Bēt Šəʾān (Hebrew Bible); Bt-šꜣr (Egyptian, New Kingdom)
status_evidence: Polybius 5.70.4; Decapolis (Pliny 5.74); Greek city coins; metropolis of Palaestina II; bishop Patrophilus at Nicaea 325
note: The gap 107-63 BC follows the Hasmonaean conquest and the exile of its people. Jewish and Samaritan minorities lived in the late Roman city. Counted as a Hellenized native town: a Ptolemaic (re)foundation is likely, but neither settlers nor a new layout are attested.
sources: Polybius 5.70.4; Josephus AJ 13.280; Tsafrir and Foerster, DOP 51 (1997); Pleiades 678378; Wikipedia: Beit She'an

other_names: Samaria (Greek); Sebaste (Herod, 27 BC); Colonia Lucia Septimia Sebaste (Septimius Severus); Sebastiya (Arabic)
site: Sebastia, Nablus Governorate
greek_from_text: Macedonian colony settled after the Samaritans killed Alexander's governor Andromachus, 331 BC (Curtius 4.8.9-11); Eusebius credits the settlement to Perdiccas
until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636. Speech: Sebaste had shrunk to a small town around the shrine of John the Baptist; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and bishops to the 6th c.; pilgrims' accounts of the shrine. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest, 634-636. Earlier John Hyrcanus besieged, took and razed Samaria, c. 108/107 BC (Josephus AJ 13.275-281)
founder: Alexander or Perdiccas (Macedonian settlers); Herod refounded it as Sebaste
refounded_by: Pompey/Gabinius 63-55 BC; Herod 27 BC (Sebaste, 6,000 settlers); Septimius Severus (colonia, c. 201)
status_evidence: Macedonian colony (Curtius; Eusebius); Herodian foundation (Josephus AJ 15.292-298); Roman colonia; see of Palaestina I (Marinus at Nicaea 325)
note: The gap 108-57 BC follows Hyrcanus' destruction. The Samaritan centre was at Shechem and Mount Gerizim, not in the Macedonian city.
sources: Curtius 4.8.9-11; Josephus AJ 13.275-281; 15.292-298; Cohen 2006 (Samaria); Pleiades 678370; Wikipedia: Sebastia, Nablus

other_names: Autocratoris (Antipas); Eirenopolis Neronias (coins, AD 68); Diocaesarea (2nd c.); Tzippori (Hebrew); Saffuriyya (Arabic)
site: Tzippori National Park, by the former village of Saffuriyya and moshav Tzippori, Northern District
greek_from_text: First city coins with Greek legends, AD 67/68 (Eirenopolis Neronias Sepphoris); Antipas had rebuilt the town as his capital, c. 4 BC (Josephus AJ 18.27)
until_text: Administration: taken in the Arab conquest of Galilee, 634/635. Speech: the town shrank to the village of Saffuriyya; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 8th c.
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions to the 6th c.; bishops of Diocaesarea to the 6th c.; damage in the Jewish revolt against Gallus (351/352) and the earthquake of 363
ended_by: No named act: taken in the Arab conquest of Galilee, 634/635
pre_greek_name: Ṣippōrī (Hebrew and Aramaic, Mishnah and Talmud)
pre_greek_note: The name is attested in Hebrew only in rabbinic texts, later than Josephus' Greek Sepphoris; it is the native name of the town.
bilingual_evidence: Greek city coins (AD 68; Diocaesarea from Hadrian to Caracalla); Greek civic institutions; Greek and Aramaic inscriptions in the 5th-c. synagogue mosaic; Greek inscriptions of the Christian town
status_evidence: Greek civic coins; Josephus; see of Palaestina II (Diocaesarea)
sources: Josephus AJ 18.27; Meyers, Netzer and Meyers, Sepphoris (1992); Pleiades 678387; Wikipedia: Sepphoris

site: Khirbat Suq Mazin, near Deir al-Balah, Deir al-Balah Governorate
greek_from_text: Listed as a city of Palaestina I by Hierocles (c. 527) and as a see of the province.
until_text: Administration: taken with the Gaza district in 'Amr ibn al-'As's conquest, 634-637. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken with the Gaza district in the Arab conquest, 634-637
bilingual_evidence: A see of the Greek-speaking church of Palaestina I in the Gaza district, where the countryside also spoke Aramaic.
status_evidence: Hierocles, Synecdemus (Palaestina I); counted as a see of Palaestina I under Caesarea in the church lists; no bishop is known to us by name.
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. The see itself is thinly attested: no bishop of Sycomazon has been found. The site at Khirbat Suq Mazin near Deir al-Balah is a proposal.
sources: Hierocles, Synecdemus (Palaestina I); Tsafrir, Di Segni & Green, TIR Iudaea-Palaestina (1994); Pleiades 688036

site: Ancient Tiberias and Hammat, south of the modern city, Northern District
greek_from_text: Founded by Herod Antipas c. AD 18-20 and named for Tiberius (Josephus AJ 18.36-38)
until_text: Administration: surrendered on terms to Shurahbil ibn Hasana, 634/635, and became the capital of the Arab district of al-Urdunn. Speech: no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 8th c.
fade_evidence: Greek synagogue and church inscriptions to the 6th-7th c.; bishops of Tiberias to the 6th c.
ended_by: No named act: surrendered to Shurahbil ibn Hasana on terms, 634/635 (Baladhuri)
