pre_greek_note: The rabbis identified Tiberias with biblical Rakkath; this is a tradition, not a firm attestation. Josephus says Antipas built it over graves.
bilingual_evidence: Greek civic institutions (a boule of 600, archon, dekaprotoi: Josephus, BJ 2.641; Life 64-69, 296); Greek city coins; Greek dedications in the Hammat Tiberias synagogue (4th c.); seat of the Jewish Patriarchate and of the Aramaic Jerusalem Talmud
status_evidence: Josephus AJ 18.36-38 and Life; Greek civic coins; see of Palaestina II
sources: Josephus AJ 18.36-38; Life 64-69; Jensen, Herod Antipas in Galilee (2006); Pleiades 678431; Wikipedia: Tiberias

other_names: Seleukeia (on coins); Abila of the Decapolis
site: Quwaylibah (Tell Abil), Irbid Governorate
greek_from_text: City coins as Seleukeia Abila, dated by the Pompeian era of 64/63 BC, and a city of the Decapolis (Pliny NH 5.74). Antiochus III took Abila in 218 BC (Polybius 5.71), but that passage says nothing of Greek speakers, and the name Seleukeia alone does not prove a Seleucid polis.
until_text: Taken by the Arabs in 635-636; the town continued under the Umayyads and was damaged by the earthquake of 749. No later evidence for Greek speech. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the basilicas (6th-7th centuries); Umayyad occupation; earthquake of 749. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 635-636.
status_evidence: Polybius 5.71; Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); city coins (Seleukeia Abila, Pompeian era); bishops; Hierocles (Palaestina II)
note: The name Seleukeia is known from the Roman-period coins; no Hellenistic Greek text of the city is known.
sources: Polybius 5.71; Mare, Abila excavations; Schurer-Vermes-Millar II, 136-137; Pleiades 677992

site: Daraa, Daraa Governorate
greek_from_text: City coins with Greek legends from the later 2nd century (Marcus Aurelius) to Gallienus, dated by the era of the province of Arabia; a polis by the 3rd century
until_text: Taken in the Arab conquest of the Hauran, 634. The see continued, but there is no evidence of Greek speech beyond the early Islamic period.
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of residents into the 6th century; the last bishop known from the councils signed at Constantinople in 553
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
bilingual_evidence: City coins showing the aniconic cult stone of Dushara (Dusares Theos); Nabataean and Arab names in the Greek inscriptions
status_evidence: City coins; Ptolemy 5.17; bishops at Seleucia 359, Constantinople 381, Chalcedon 451 and Constantinople 553
note: Coin dates for the start of civic issues vary; the polis is secure by the Severan period.
sources: Spijkerman, The Coins of the Decapolis and Provincia Arabia (1978); Sartre, D'Alexandre a Zenobie; Pleiades 678002

site: As-Sanamayn, Daraa Governorate
greek_from_text: Bishop Sopater 'of Errhe' among the bishops of Arabia at the Council of Nicaea, 325; the see is probably Aere, whose residents' Greek inscriptions go back to the 2nd c. (temple of Tyche, 191), when it was a village.
until_text: Administration: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the temple of Tyche (191) and of the village. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
bilingual_evidence: Greek dedications of residents with Arab names at the temple of Tyche (AD 191) and other Greek inscriptions of the village.
status_evidence: A see of Arabia named Erra/Errhe: bishop Sopater at Nicaea 325 (list of signatories); titular see 'Erra'. Aere was a large village and road station on the Damascus-Bostra road with Greek inscriptions of its residents.
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts) as a see of the Greek-speaking church, and here Greek inscriptions of the residents are known. But the identification of the see of Erra with Aere (as-Sanamayn) is only a proposal; if it is wrong, Aere was a village. Vailhe reads the see's name in the Notitia Antiochena as Erra or Hierapolis.
sources: Wikipedia: Arabia Petraea (titular sees); Pleiades 678004

other_names: Metrocomia ('mother-village') of the Bacatheni (church lists); Safut? (Arabic)
site: Safut, north-west of Amman, Balqa Governorate (tentative)
greek_from_text: Bishop Alypius of Bacatha at the second Council of Ephesus, 449.
until_text: Administration: taken in the conquest of the Balqa, 634-636. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishop Anthony, 649, after the conquest. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Balqa, 634-636; its bishop Anthony still corresponded with Rome in 649.
bilingual_evidence: A 'mother-village' of the Philadelphene (Epiphanius) with bishops of the Greek-speaking church from 449 to 649.
status_evidence: See with bishops Alypius (Ephesus 449), Gregory (451 or 518; the lists differ), Barachus (532/536) and Anthony (letters with Pope Martin I, 649) (Le Quien; Fedalto); listed as 'Metrocomia' under Petra and as Bacatha in the lists of Arabia; Epiphanius (Panarion) calls Bacatha a metrokomia of the Philadelphene.
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. A large village (metrokomia) that became a see, like Neila. The site is unknown; Safut near as-Salt is a tentative identification, so the point is only regional. The church lists put it under Petra or under Bostra; the two entries are probably one see.
sources: Wikipedia: Bacatha in Palaestina; Wikipedia (it): Arcidiocesi di Bosra; Le Quien, Oriens Christianus III; Epiphanius, Panarion 58

site: Busan, Suwayda Governorate
greek_from_text: A Greek inscription names its bishop Menas, 573
until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635; there is no later Greek evidence. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Inscription of bishop Menas (573). Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
bilingual_evidence: Village of the Jabal al-Arab with Arab names in its Greek inscriptions; Safaitic texts in the steppe nearby
status_evidence: Bishop attested in an inscription (573); titular see 'Bosana'
note: A village with a bishop late in the 6th century; whether this was a full see or a rural bishop is unclear.
sources: Wikipedia: Bosana (Syria); Pleiades 678071

other_names: Nea Traiane Bostra (from 106); Colonia Bostra (under Severus Alexander); Busra (Nabataean bṣrʾ); Busra al-Sham (Arabic)
site: Busra al-Sham, Daraa Governorate
greek_from_text: Made capital of the new province of Arabia as Nea Traiane Bostra when Trajan annexed the Nabataean kingdom, 106
until_text: Administration: Bostra was the first Syrian city to surrender to the Arabs, 634. Speech: Greek inscriptions of residents continue through the 6th century; the Melkite see lasted, but the town became Arabic-speaking in the 8th-9th centuries.
fade_evidence: Greek building inscriptions of the 6th century (cathedral 512/513); a Greek-writing bishop Stephen early 8th century (Le Quien); Arabic inscriptions from the Umayyad period
ended_by: Surrendered to Khalid ibn al-Walid, with Shurahbil ibn Hasana, 634 (al-Baladhuri); no named act ended Greek speech.
pre_greek_note: The Amarna Busruna is usually identified with Bostra.
bilingual_evidence: Nabataean royal city under Rabbel II with Nabataean inscriptions into the 2nd century; the cult of Dushara-A'ra and the games Actia Dusaria; Arabic speakers in town and countryside; Greek civic inscriptions, coins and clergy
status_evidence: Provincial capital of Arabia from 106; city coins; Roman colonia; metropolitan see of Arabia; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena
note: Greek became the language of public life only after 106; the Nabataean and Arab population stayed.
sources: Sartre, Bostra (1985); IGLS XIII.1; Millar, The Roman Near East; Pleiades 678073

other_names: Septimia Canatha (colonia under Septimius Severus); Gabinia (?); Qanawat (Arabic)
site: Qanawat, Suwayda Governorate
greek_from_text: Coins dated by the Pompeian era of 64/63 BC; one of the cities of the Decapolis (Pliny NH 5.74)
until_text: Passed to the Arabs in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. Greek inscriptions of residents run into the 6th century; there is no evidence of Greek speech after the early Islamic period.
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the temple of Zeus Megistos and of the churches built into the 'Seraya'; bishops of Canatha at the councils
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635.
refounded_by: Pompey (era of 64/63 BC); Septimius Severus (colonia Septimia Canatha)
pre_greek_note: The identification of biblical Kenath with Qanawat is traditional but not proven.
bilingual_evidence: Nabataean inscriptions at Canatha and at the nearby sanctuary of Si'; Safaitic and Arab names in the district
status_evidence: City coins (Claudius to Domitian) with the Pompeian era; Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); Ptolemy 5.15; Josephus BJ 1.366 (battle of Canatha, 32 BC); bishop's see of Arabia
note: Some scholars distinguish Kanatha at Qanawat from a second Kanata at al-Kerak in the Hauran and give the Decapolis coins to one or the other; Qanawat is the usual identification.
sources: Pliny NH 5.74; Spijkerman 1978; Schurer-Vermes-Millar II, 140-142; Pleiades 678082

site: Buraq, northern edge of the Lajat, Rif Dimashq Governorate
greek_from_text: Bishop Chilon of Constantia at the Council of Constantinople, 381 (Le Quien put him at Nicaea, wrongly). The name honours the house of Constantine, but the dynastic name alone is not evidence.
until_text: Administration: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
founder: an emperor of the house of Constantine (the name only)
bilingual_evidence: A see of the province of Arabia, where the villagers of the Hauran set up Greek inscriptions with Arab names.
status_evidence: See of Arabia under Bostra: bishops Chilon at Constantinople 381 and Solemus at Chalcedon 451 (Mansi); Notitia Antiochena. Waddington identified it 'with much likelihood' with Buraq, which had its own era and inscriptions of building works under Constantine.
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts) as a see of the Greek-speaking church. If Waddington's identification with Buraq on the northern edge of the Lajat is right, the town's own inscriptions are known; it is not proven.
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia: Constantia (Arabia); Waddington, Inscriptions de Syrie; Pleiades 678077

site: Tell al-Ash'ari, Daraa Governorate (proposed)
greek_from_text: Stephanus of Byzantium calls Dion a foundation of Alexander; the Macedonian name points to early Hellenistic settlers. First secure mention: taken by Alexander Jannaeus, c. 83 BC (Josephus AJ 13.393)
until_text: Freed by Pompey in 63 BC; coins under the Severans. Its later history is little known; no evidence for Greek speech after the Arab conquest. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: City coins of the Severan period dated by the Pompeian era; a see 'Dia' in some lists. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken by Alexander Jannaeus c. 83 BC and freed by Pompey in 63 BC; it passed to the Arabs in 634-636.
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); Ptolemy 5.15; Josephus AJ 13.393, 14.75; city coins (Septimius Severus to Caracalla)
note: The site is disputed: Tell al-Ash'ari in Syria, on the slopes of the Yarmuk valley, is generally assumed (two coins of Dion found in a tomb there); Kropp has suggested that the town centre lay at nearby Tafas, and Husn and Tell al-Husn in Jordan have also been proposed. The Alexander foundation may be a later claim. The coins (Septimius Severus to Caracalla, AD 204-208) use the Pompeian era of 64/63 BC.
sources: Stephanus of Byzantium s.v. Dion; Cohen 2006, 245-247; Schurer-Vermes-Millar II, 148-149; Pleiades 682543

site: Al-Suwayda, Suwayda Governorate
greek_from_text: Soada received civic status as Dionysias under Commodus, c. 180-185; Greek was already used beside Nabataean in the 1st century BC
until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634. No evidence of Greek speech after the early Islamic period.
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the basilica and of residents into the 6th century; bishops of Dionysias in the 5th-6th centuries
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634.
bilingual_evidence: A Greek-Nabataean bilingual tomb inscription (Hamrat, 1st c. BC); Arab names in the Greek inscriptions
status_evidence: Ptolemy 5.15; city inscriptions (a "lord builder Dionysos" honoured as founder); bishops Severus at Nicaea 325, Elpidius at Constantinople 381 and Maras at Chalcedon 451, and Peter in an inscription (Waddington 2327); Hierocles 723; Georgius Cyprius 1072; Notitia Antiochena (under Bostra)
note: The grant of civic status under Commodus rests on inscriptions as read by Sartre and others; the exact year is not fixed.
sources: Sartre, D'Alexandre a Zenobie; IGLS XVI (Djebel al-Arab); Pleiades 678119

site: Tell Hisban, Amman Governorate
greek_from_text: City coins of Elagabalus (218-222) with Greek legends; Herod had fortified the place earlier (Josephus AJ 15.294)
until_text: Passed to the Arabs in the conquest of the Balqa' (634-636); the see continued, but there is no evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period.
fade_evidence: Greek mosaic inscriptions of churches (6th century); bishops of Esbus from 431; the mosaicist Staurachios 'of Esbus' signed the Greek floor of St Stephen at Umm ar-Rasas (756/785)
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Balqa', 634-636.
bilingual_evidence: Arab and Nabataean names in the Greek inscriptions of the district; Herod settled soldiers in the Esebonitis
status_evidence: City coins of Elagabalus; Ptolemy 5.16; bishop Zosys at Ephesus 431; Hierocles (Arabia)
sources: Spijkerman 1978; Geraty and others, Hesban excavations; Pleiades 697662

other_names: Antiocheia and Seleukeia (Seleucid names); Pompeia; Umm Qais (Arabic)
site: Umm Qais, Irbid Governorate
greek_from_text: Taken by Antiochus III in 218 BC as the strongest place in the district (Polybius 5.71); Menippus the Cynic was born there in the 3rd century BC
until_text: Destroyed after a ten-month siege by Alexander Jannaeus c. 100 BC and rebuilt by Pompey in 63 BC. Taken by the Arabs in 635-636; Umayyad occupation; damaged by the earthquake of 749, after which the town declined. The baths of Gadara at Hammat Gader were restored in 662 with a Greek inscription naming Mu'awiya and John of Gadara as the local supervisor, so the town's Greek is attested after the conquest. The date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750; the range starts at 662.
fade_evidence: The Greek writers Menippus, Meleager, Philodemus, Theodorus and Oenomaus; Greek inscriptions of churches into the 6th-7th centuries; earthquake of 749. Greek building inscription of 5 December 662 (year 726 of the city, 42 of the Arabs) at Hammat Gader, the baths of Gadara: restored under Mu'awiya by the governor 'Abd Allah son of Abu Hashim, with John of Gadara supervising the work (Green and Tsafrir 1982; Hasson 1982). Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: Destroyed by Alexander Jannaeus, c. 100 BC; rebuilt by Pompey, 63 BC. Passed to the Arabs in 635-636 (no named act for the city).
refounded_by: Pompey 63 BC (for his freedman Demetrius of Gadara)
status_evidence: Polybius 5.71; Josephus AJ 13.356, BJ 1.155; Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); city coins; bishops at Nicaea 325 and later; Hierocles (Palaestina II)
note: Meleager calls Gadara 'Attic among the Syrians'. The founder of the Hellenistic city is not known.
sources: Polybius 5.71; Josephus BJ 1.155; Schurer-Vermes-Millar II, 132-136; Pleiades 678142

site: Jerash, Jerash Governorate
greek_from_text: City era from Pompey's settlement of 63 BC and a city of the Decapolis (Pliny NH 5.74). The name Antiocheia on the Chrysorhoas points to a renaming under Antiochus IV (175-164 BC), but the name alone does not prove a Greek polis, and the Hellenistic remains are not Greek texts; local traditions of Alexander or Perdiccas as founder are legends.
until_text: Administration: taken by the Arabs in 634/635; an Umayyad provincial town with a mosque beside the churches. Speech: Greek inscriptions of residents run to 611 (church of Bishop Genesius). The earthquake of 18 January 749 wrecked the town, but it lived on as a smaller Abbasid settlement. With no Greek evidence of its own after the conquest, the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek church inscriptions to 611 (church of Bishop Genesius); Umayyad mosque and houses; earthquake of 18 January 749. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: Taken in the Arab conquest of 634/635, probably by troops under Shurahbil ibn Hasana; the earthquake of 749 ruined the town.
pre_greek_note: Bronze and Iron Age remains lie under the city; no pre-Greek name is attested in non-Greek sources.
bilingual_evidence: Nabataean and Arab names and a few Nabataean inscriptions in the Roman period; the countryside spoke Aramaic and Arabic
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); city coins; boule and demos in many Greek inscriptions; bishops at Seleucia 359 and Chalcedon 451; Hierocles (Arabia)
note: Counted as a Hellenized native town: the Seleucid renaming is not matched by attested settlers, and the claims of Macedonian origin (Alexander, Perdiccas) are later civic traditions. Greek institutions are secure from the 1st century BC.
sources: Kraeling (ed.), Gerasa: City of the Decapolis (1938); Cohen 2006, 248-253; Seigne, Jerash (various); Pleiades 678158

site: Shaqqa, Suwayda Governorate
greek_from_text: The village of Saccaea became the city of Maximianopolis under the Tetrarchs, c. 286-305; Greek inscriptions of residents from the 2nd century
until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634. No evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period.
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the 'Kaisariye' and of churches; bishops of Maximianopolis in Arabia
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634.
bilingual_evidence: Arab names in the Greek inscriptions; a village of the Trachonitis-Hauran raised to a city
status_evidence: Renamed city under the Tetrarchs; bishop's see of Arabia (councils; Notitia Antiochena)
sources: Sartre, D'Alexandre a Zenobie; Le Quien, Oriens Christianus II; Pleiades 678366

site: Madaba, Madaba Governorate
greek_from_text: City coins with Greek legends under the Severans (early 3rd century)
until_text: Administration: passed to the Arabs in 634-636. Speech: the Christian community still laid floors with Greek inscriptions under the Umayyads and early Abbasids (Church of the Virgin, 767); the town declined in the 9th century.
fade_evidence: Madaba mosaic map (6th century); Greek mosaic inscriptions to 767 (Church of the Virgin) and at nearby Umm ar-Rasas (718, 756)
ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 634-636; the community dwindled in the 9th century.
bilingual_evidence: Nabataean inscriptions of the 1st century AD; Arab names in the Greek mosaic inscriptions
status_evidence: City coins (Severan period); bishops of Medaba (councils); Hierocles (Arabia)
note: The latest Greek mosaic inscriptions may have been written by Arabic-speaking Christians; the end date is an estimate.
sources: Piccirillo, The Mosaics of Jordan (1993); Spijkerman 1978; Pleiades 697701

site: Khirbet en-Nila (proposed), As-Suwayda Governorate
greek_from_text: Listed as a see of Arabia under Bostra in the Notitia Antiochena (c. 570), as 'Neila or Nilakome'.
until_text: Administration: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
bilingual_evidence: A see of the province of Arabia in the Hauran, where villagers set up Greek inscriptions with Arab names.
status_evidence: A see of Arabia under Bostra in the Notitia Antiochena ('Neila or Nilakome', Vailhe); titular see Neila; 'Nelkomia/Neela?' in the Barrington Atlas (69 E4).
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. A village (kome) that became a see; the site follows the Barrington Atlas, which marks it with a question mark.
sources: Wikipedia (it): Arcidiocesi di Bosra; Pleiades 678305; Devreesse 1945

site: Nawa, Daraa Governorate
greek_from_text: Its bishop Petronius attended the Council of Ephesus in 431 (Jobius at Chalcedon, 451); Greek inscriptions of residents are known from the town
until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. No evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period; the district became Arabic-speaking.
fade_evidence: Greek funerary and building inscriptions (Roman and late Roman); bishops of Neve at the councils
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
other_language: Aramaic (including a Jewish community) and Arabic
bilingual_evidence: A Jewish community with a synagogue (remains and Aramaic inscriptions); Arab and Aramaic names in the Greek inscriptions
status_evidence: Bishops Petronius at Ephesus 431 and Jobius at Chalcedon 451; Notitia Antiochena (under Bostra); Georgius Cyprius; Greek inscriptions (Revue biblique 3, 625)
note: A large Hauran town that became a see; its first known bishop is from 431.
sources: Le Quien, Oriens Christianus II; Wikipedia: Nawa, Syria; Pleiades 678307

site: Al-Mismiyah, northern Lajat, Daraa Governorate
greek_from_text: The metrokomia ("chief village") of the Trachonitis in a Greek edict of the governor Julius Saturninus, 185-187 (OGIS 609); a bishop's see whose bishops attended Ephesus (431) and Chalcedon (451)
until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. No evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period; the district became Arabic-speaking.
fade_evidence: Greek edict of Julius Saturninus; the 'praetorium' temple of 160-169 with Greek inscriptions; bishops of Phaena
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
bilingual_evidence: The 'metrokomia of the Trachon' with Arab names in its Greek inscriptions
status_evidence: Metrokomia of the Trachon (OGIS 609, on the temple); many Greek inscriptions of residents; bishops at Ephesus 431 and Chalcedon 451
note: A chief village rather than a polis in the Roman period; counted from its first known bishop, 431.
sources: OGIS 609; Wikipedia: Phaena; Pleiades 678328

site: Amman Citadel and downtown, Amman Governorate
greek_from_text: Zeno Cotylas, a ruler with a Greek name, held Philadelphia as its tyrant c. 135 BC (Josephus AJ 13.235; BJ 1.60). Ptolemy II (285-246 BC) had renamed Rabbath-Ammon after himself (Stephanus; Jerome), but the Zenon papyri (259 BC) still call the district the Ammanitis and Polybius (5.71) calls the town Rabbatamana in 218 BC.
until_text: Administration: taken by the Arabs c. 635-636; an Umayyad governor's seat with a palace on the citadel. Speech: Greek-speaking Christians lived there into the Umayyad period; the earthquake of 749 damaged the town, and Arabic replaced Greek by the 9th century. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of churches in the 6th-7th centuries; Umayyad citadel; earthquake of 749. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act recorded for the city: it passed to the Arabs in the conquest of 635-636.
pre_greek_name: Rabbat Bnê ʿAmmôn (Hebrew Bible); Bīt-Ammān (Akkadian, the kingdom)
bilingual_evidence: Nabataean and Arab names in Greek inscriptions; Arabic-speaking countryside; Christian Palestinian Aramaic in the region
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); city coins with Greek legends; Greek civic inscriptions; bishop's see of Arabia; Hierocles
note: Ptolemaic soldiers settled in the district (Zenon papyri), but settlers in the city itself are not directly attested, so it is counted as a Hellenized native town. The renaming is known only from later writers; the Zenon papyri and Polybius still use the native name.
sources: Cohen 2006, 268-272; Polybius 5.71; Schurer-Vermes-Millar II, 155-158; Pleiades 697728

site: Shahba, Suwayda Governorate
greek_from_text: Philip the Arab founded the city at his birthplace, 244-249 (Aurelius Victor 28.1), laid out with walls, theatre and baths
until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634. The town shrank; no evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period.
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and mosaics of the 3rd-4th centuries; bishops of Philippopolis in Arabia
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634.
bilingual_evidence: Founded at the native village of the emperor Philip 'the Arab'; Arab names in the Greek inscriptions of residents
status_evidence: Aurelius Victor 28.1; city coins of Philip; colonia; bishop's see of Arabia
note: A new imperial foundation on a village site; It could also be counted a Greek city, as a Roman foundation.
sources: Aurelius Victor 28.1; Wikipedia: Shahba; Pleiades 678332

site: unlocated; Pleiades places it at the Raphon of 1 Maccabees in the Hauran, Daraa Governorate
greek_from_text: Listed among the cities of the Decapolis by Pliny (NH 5.74); the Raphon of 1 Maccabees 5:37 was then a settlement, not a known polis
until_text: Known only from Pliny and Ptolemy; no later civic evidence. It may have merged into the territory of another city.
fade_evidence: No inscriptions or coins securely assigned; not in the late Roman lists
ended_by: No named act: the city drops out of the record after the 2nd century.
status_evidence: Pliny NH 5.74 (Decapolis); Ptolemy 5.15
note: The location is uncertain: proposals include the Raphon of 1 Maccabees in the Hauran and a site south of Damascus; the Decapolis listing is the only evidence of civic status.
sources: Pliny NH 5.74; Schurer-Vermes-Millar II, 137; Pleiades 678360

site: Izra', Daraa Governorate
greek_from_text: A bishop's see of Arabia by the 6th century; Greek dedication of the church of St George by John son of Diomedes, 515
until_text: Taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635. No evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period; the district became Arabic-speaking.
fade_evidence: Greek inscription of the church of St George (515) and of the church of St Elias (542)
ended_by: No named act: taken in the conquest of the Hauran, 634-635 (Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaign).
bilingual_evidence: Greek building inscriptions of residents with Arab and Aramaic names; the Christian community still worships in the 6th-century church
status_evidence: Greek dedication of the church of St George, 515, by John son of Diomedes, a proteuon (leading councillor) of the town (IGLS XV 244); bishop's see of Arabia (Le Quien; titular see Zorava)
note: Counted as a village that became a see; its Christian community, now Arabic-speaking, is continuous.
sources: Wikipedia: Izra'; Le Quien, Oriens Christianus II; Pleiades 678459

other_names: Aelana; Ailana; Berenike (Josephus); Ayla (Arabic); Elath (Hebrew Bible)
site: Aqaba, Aqaba Governorate
greek_from_text: A city and bishopric by 325, when its bishop attended Nicaea; garrison of Legio X Fretensis from c. 300; earliest purpose-built church (late 3rd century)
until_text: Its lord John son of Ru'ba made a treaty with Muhammad at Tabuk in 630; an Islamic walled town (Ayla) was built beside the old one c. 650. No later evidence for Greek speech. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Church of c. 300; bishops of Aila to the 6th century; the new Islamic town of Ayla (c. 650). Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: John son of Ru'ba, lord of Ayla, submitted to Muhammad by treaty at Tabuk, 630 (Ibn Ishaq); the caliphate built a new town beside it c. 650.
pre_greek_note: Biblical Elath is often placed at Tell el-Kheleifeh nearby rather than under Aila itself.
bilingual_evidence: Nabataean port; its Christian lord in 630, John son of Ru'ba, bore a Greek name and an Arab patronym
status_evidence: Bishop at Nicaea 325; Hierocles (Palaestina III); Notitia Antiochena
note: Greek-speaking residents are inferred mainly from the church and garrison; the population was largely Nabataean and Arab.
sources: Parker, The Roman Aqaba Project; Whitcomb, Ayla; Pleiades 746700

site: Tel Arad, west of the modern town of Arad, Southern District
greek_from_text: Bishop Stephen of Arad at the synod of Jerusalem, 518 (Le Quien).
until_text: Administration: passed to the Arabs with the Negev in the 630s. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Last bishop known: Stephen, 536. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs with the Negev in the 630s.
pre_greek_name: 'Arad (Hebrew Bible; Egyptian 'rd in Shoshenq I's list)
bilingual_evidence: A village of the Negev that became a see of Palaestina III.
status_evidence: See of Palaestina III under Petra: bishop Stephen at the synods of Jerusalem, 518 and 536 (Le Quien); Eusebius (Onomasticon) calls Arad a village.
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. A village that became a see; the late Roman settlement is placed at or near Tel Arad, whose Hellenistic Greek ostraca belong to a garrison.
sources: Le Quien, Oriens Christianus III; Eusebius, Onomasticon; Wikipedia (it): Diocesi di Arad; Pleiades 87764825

site: Al-Rabba, Karak Governorate
greek_from_text: City coins with Greek legends (Rabbathmoba-Areopolis) under the Severans; a Greek census return of 127 in the Babatha archive was filed there
until_text: Passed to the Arabs in 634-636. The see continued for a time; there is no evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions of the 4th-6th centuries; bishops of Areopolis; the city on the Madaba map. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 634-636.
pre_greek_note: Greek 'Areopolis' was linked to biblical Ar of Moab; the identification is uncertain.
bilingual_evidence: A Nabataean town of Moab; Babatha's documents (Greek and Aramaic, 2nd century) were registered at Rabbathmoba; Arab names in its Greek inscriptions
status_evidence: City coins (Severans); Babatha papyri (P.Yadin 16); bishops; Hierocles (Palaestina III)
sources: Spijkerman 1978; Yadin and others, The Documents from the Bar Kokhba Period (P.Yadin 16); Pleiades 697632

site: Gharandal, Tafilah Governorate
greek_from_text: Its bishops are listed from 431 (Gams, after Le Quien).
until_text: Administration: passed to the Arabs in 634-636; the neighbouring towns of Adhruh and Jarba had made treaties with Muhammad in 630. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Last bishop known: 536. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 634-636; the neighbouring towns of Adhruh and Jarba had made treaties with Muhammad in 630 (Ibn Ishaq).
bilingual_evidence: A see of Palaestina III in an Arab and Nabataean district.
status_evidence: See of Palaestina III under Petra, with bishops from 431 to 536 (Le Quien; Gams); Hierocles.
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known.
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia: Arindela; Le Quien, Oriens Christianus III; Pleiades 697633

site: Udhruh, Ma'an Governorate
greek_from_text: Bishop John of Augustopolis at the Council of Ephesus, 431.
until_text: Administration: the people of Adhruh made a treaty with Muhammad during the Tabuk expedition, 630; the region passed to the Arabs in 634-636. Speech: no evidence of the town's own after the conquest; the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishop John, 536; the Petra papyri (6th c.). Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia go on to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720; Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); the Nessana papyri are in Greek to c. 690; the Melkites of the region turned to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: The people of Adhruh submitted to Muhammad by treaty during the Tabuk expedition, 630 (Ibn Ishaq; al-Waqidi).
bilingual_evidence: A see of Palaestina III beside a legionary fortress; the Greek Petra papyri (6th c.) name the place.
status_evidence: See of Palaestina III under Petra: bishop John at Ephesus 431; a second John at the synod of Jerusalem, 536; Hierocles; Notitia Antiochena.
note: Counted as a see of the Greek-speaking church (in the Levant every see counts); no Greek inscription of its own residents is known. Augustopolis is usually placed at Udhruh, a legionary fortress with a small town and a church outside its walls; the identification is common but not certain.
sources: Wikipedia: Augustopolis in Palaestina; Le Quien, Oriens Christianus III; Pleiades 697625

site: Al-Karak, Karak Governorate
greek_from_text: City coins with Greek legends under the Severans
until_text: Passed to the Arabs in 634-636. A Christian community survived into the Crusader and Ottoman periods, Arabic-speaking; there is no evidence for Greek speech after the early Islamic period. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: City shown on the Madaba map; bishops of Charachmoba; the later Christians of Karak used Arabic. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in 634-636.
pre_greek_name: Qîr-Ḥareśet / Qîr Môʾāb (Hebrew Bible, 2 Kings 3:25; Isaiah 15:1)
bilingual_evidence: A Nabataean and then Arab town of Moab; the Greek name keeps the Aramaic karka, 'fortified town'
status_evidence: City coins (Severans); Ptolemy 5.16; bishops; Hierocles (Palaestina III)
sources: Spijkerman 1978; Wikipedia: Kerak; Pleiades 697648

site: Halutza (Khalasa) ruins, Ramat HaNegev, Southern District
greek_from_text: Greek city by the 4th c.: Zenobius and other rhetors from Elusa; listed by Ptolemy (5.16.10) as a town of Idumaea; a Nabataean town since the 2nd c. BC
until_text: Administration: the Negev came under the caliphs in the 630s. Speech: Greek papyri at nearby Nessana run to c. 690, when Arabic took over the tax documents; Elusa was abandoned by the 8th c.
fade_evidence: Nessana papyri (Greek to c. 690; Greek-Arabic bilingual documents from the 670s); abandonment of the town in the 7th-8th c.
ended_by: No named act: the Negev came under the caliphs in the 630s; Greek gave way to Arabic in the documents by c. 690 and the town was abandoned
pre_greek_note: A Nabataean inscription of the 2nd c. BC found at Elusa names a king Aretas; no non-Greek form of the town's name older than the rabbinic Halutza is attested.
bilingual_evidence: The sophist Zenobius of Elusa taught Greek rhetoric at Antioch (d. 354) and Libanius writes of rhetors from Elusa; Greek inscriptions and papyri; in Jerome's Life of Hilarion (25) the townspeople greet Hilarion in 'Syriac', a Semitic tongue, and worship Venus
status_evidence: Ptolemy 5.16.10; Hierocles (Palaestina III); see of Palaestina III with bishops from the 5th c.; Madaba map; Nessana papyri
note: Some scholars think Elusa was the capital of Palaestina III for a time.
sources: Jerome, Life of Hilarion 25; Libanius, Letters; Kraemer, Excavations at Nessana III (1958); Pleiades 687890; Wikipedia: Halutza

site: Mamshit National Park, near Dimona, Southern District
greek_from_text: First attested as a city in late antiquity: Hierocles lists Mampsis in Palaestina III; Greek church inscriptions of the late 4th-5th c.
until_text: Administration and speech ended together: the town was abandoned in the 7th c., around the Arab conquest of the Negev.
fade_evidence: Late Roman churches and houses; abandonment in the 7th c.
ended_by: No named act: the town was abandoned around the Arab conquest of the 630s
bilingual_evidence: Greek mosaic inscriptions in its two churches (late 4th-5th c.) and Greek epitaphs; a Nabataean town in origin with Arab names among its people
status_evidence: Hierocles (Palaestina III); Eusebius, Onomasticon; see of Palaestina III
note: A small walled town; its civic rank rests on Hierocles and the church lists.
sources: Negev, The Architecture of Mampsis (1988); Hierocles, Synecdemus (Palaestina III); Pleiades 687963; Wikipedia: Mamshit

other_names: Reqem (Nabataean rqmw); Hadriane Petra Metropolis; Colonia Antoniniana Petra
site: Petra, beside the town of Wadi Musa, Ma'an Governorate
greek_from_text: Annexed by Trajan in 106 and made a metropolis (Hadriane Petra Metropolis from 114 or 130); Greek was already used in Nabataean Petra for some inscriptions in the 1st century
until_text: Capital of Palaestina III. The city declined after the earthquakes of 363 and 551; the Greek Petra papyri end in the 590s; there is no record of its conquest, and the town was largely abandoned by the 7th-8th century.
fade_evidence: Petra papyri (537-593), burnt in the church c. 600; Greek inscriptions of the churches; earthquakes of 363 and 551
ended_by: No named act: the city declined after the earthquakes of 363 and 551; the Arab conquest of the 630s is not recorded for Petra.
bilingual_evidence: Nabataean royal capital with Nabataean inscriptions to the 4th century; the Petra papyri (6th century) are Greek documents of landowners with Arabic names and Arabic field names
status_evidence: Nabataean capital; metropolis of Arabia; city coins; Roman colonia; metropolitan see of Palaestina III; Hierocles; Petra papyri
note: Greek became a main language only under Roman rule; Nabataean Aramaic and Arabic stayed in use.
sources: Frosen and others, The Petra Papyri I-V; Millar, The Roman Near East; Pleiades 697725

site: Khirbet Faynan, Wadi Araba, Tafilah Governorate
greek_from_text: A see of Palaestina III by the 5th century; earlier a mining settlement where Christian convicts worked in the 300s
until_text: Mining and the town declined in the 7th century; passed to the Arabs in the 630s. No later evidence for Greek speech.
fade_evidence: Greek Christian tombstones from the cemetery; bishops of Phaeno (5th-6th centuries)
ended_by: No named act: the mining town declined and passed to the Arabs in the 630s.
bilingual_evidence: Copper mines worked by convicts, including Christians from Egypt and Palestine (Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine 7, 13); Greek Christian tombstones; a local Arab population
status_evidence: Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine; bishops of Phaeno; Hierocles (Palaestina III)
note: A mining settlement that became a see; whether it was a city in more than the church's sense is doubtful.
sources: Eusebius, Martyrs of Palestine 7.2, 13; Barker and others, Wadi Faynan; Pleiades 697726

other_names: Zoora; Segor; Zoar (Hebrew Bible); Ghor es-Safi (Arabic)
site: Ghor es-Safi, southeast of the Dead Sea, Karak Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek legal documents of residents of the district of Zoara in the Babatha archive, from 110
until_text: A see of Palaestina III. Greek Christian tombstones dated by the era of Arabia run from the 4th to at least the 6th century. Passed to the Arabs in the 630s; the later Islamic town of Zughar was Arabic-speaking. No evidence of the town's own after the conquest: the date is the estimate for Palestine and Transjordan, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek tombstones of the an-Naq cemetery (mid-4th to 6th century and later); Jewish Aramaic tombstones (4th-6th centuries); the city on the Madaba map. Regional markers: Greek church inscriptions of Palestine and Arabia to the 760s-780s (Ma'in 719/720, Umm ar-Rasas 718 and 756/785); Nessana papyri in Greek to c. 690; the Melkite turn to Arabic in the 9th c.
ended_by: No named act: passed to the Arabs in the 630s.
bilingual_evidence: The Babatha archive (Mahoza in the district of Zoara, 110-132) in Greek, Nabataean and Jewish Aramaic; Jewish Aramaic tombstones and some 400 Greek Christian tombstones from the town
status_evidence: Babatha papyri; Ptolemy 5.16 (Zoara); bishops of Zoara; Hierocles (Palaestina III)
note: Whether Zoara was a polis in the 2nd century is unclear; it is secure as a see by the 4th-5th century.
sources: Meimaris and Kritikakou-Nikolaropoulou, Inscriptions from Palaestina Tertia Ia (2005); Yadin and others, The Documents from the Bar Kokhba Period; Politis, Ghor es-Safi; Pleiades 697768

site: unlocated; on the Pallacopas canal west of the Euphrates, towards the Arabian side, perhaps near Najaf or Kufa, Najaf Governorate
greek_from_text: In spring 323 BC Alexander sailed down the Pallacopas canal, founded and walled a city there and settled in it Greek mercenaries who volunteered and men unfit for service by age or wounds (Arrian, Anab. 7.21.7)
until_text: Never mentioned again after Arrian's account of its foundation; it probably did not survive long after Alexander's death. Some identify it with the Alexandria near Babylon of the Alexander Romance.
fade_evidence: Only Arrian 7.21.7 (from Aristobulus); no later trace
ended_by: No named act: the town is not heard of after its foundation
status_evidence: Alexander foundation with Greek settlers (Arrian, Anab. 7.21.7); Cohen 2013
note: A real foundation with Greek settlers, but unlocated and without any later history; the phase is given as the foundation year only, with the possible end in the range.
sources: Arrian, Anabasis 7.21.7; Cohen 2013 (Alexandreia on the Pallakopas); Wikipedia: List of cities founded by Alexander the Great

other_names: Weh-Andiyok-Khosrow, 'Khosrow's better Antioch' (Middle Persian); Rumagan (Persian); al-Rumiyya (Arabic); perhaps Mahoze Hadatta, 'the New City' (Syriac)
site: near Salman Pak (al-Mada'in), Baghdad Governorate; exact site not identified
greek_from_text: Khosrow I founded it near Ctesiphon for the people of Antioch whom he had taken captive in 540 (Procopius, Wars 2.14.1-4; al-Tabari)
until_text: The captives of Antioch were Greek speakers; the town still had about 30,000 people in the late 6th c., and John of Ephesus (writing to the 580s) knows it. No Greek text from the town survives, and its people lived among Syriac- and Persian-speaking neighbours, so Greek speech probably faded within a few generations. The Arabs took it by treaty with the other towns of al-Mada'in in 637; as al-Rumiyya it was briefly the residence of the caliph al-Mansur in 754-755, when Abu Muslim was killed there, and it was deserted by the 10th c.
fade_evidence: Procopius, Wars 2.14 (540s); John of Ephesus, HE III.6.19 (late 6th c.) still names the city; the Arabic name al-Rumiyya, 'the Roman (town)', recalls its origin
ended_by: No named act for Greek speech, which is not attested after the late 6th c. In the Arab conquest of al-Mada'in the vanguard of Khalid ibn Urfuta, in the army of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, made a treaty with the people of al-Rumiyya, who could leave or stay and pay tribute; Sa'd entered al-Mada'in in March 637 (al-Tabari; Encyclopaedia Iranica: Madaen)
other_language: Syriac (deportees from Sura, Callinicum and Batnae and the local population)
bilingual_evidence: Procopius (Wars 2.14.1-4): Khosrow I settled the captives of Antioch here, built them a bath and a hippodrome and brought their charioteers and musicians; Jacob of Edessa names captives from Antioch, Sura, Beroea, Apamea, Callinicum and Batnae
status_evidence: Royal Sasanian foundation laid out on the plan of Antioch, with bath and hippodrome (Procopius, Wars 2.14; al-Tabari); about 30,000 inhabitants in the late 6th c.
note: A town built for captives. Classed as bilingual because the deportees came from both Greek- and Syriac-speaking towns.
sources: Procopius, Wars 2.14.1-4; Encyclopaedia Iranica: Deportations; Encyclopaedia Iranica: Madaen; Wikipedia: Weh Antiok Khosrow; Canepa 2009, The Two Eyes of the Earth

other_names: Chalasar (its name in Isidore's day, Parthian Stations 2)
site: Karastel, near Baqubah, Diyala Governorate; identification probable
greek_from_text: First attested through the Greek historian Apollodorus of Artemita, author of the Parthika, c. 100 BC (Strabo 2.5.12, 11.7.3, 11.11.1); probably a Seleucid foundation of the 3rd c. BC
until_text: Isidore of Charax (Parthian Stations 2, c. AD 1) calls it 'a Greek city' on the Silla river. By AD 36 Tacitus (Ann. 6.41) lists Halus and Artemita as 'Parthian towns', in contrast with the 'Macedonian' foundations, which may mean that Greek no longer marked it. Later the Sasanian palace town of Dastagird lay nearby.
fade_evidence: Apollodorus of Artemita, c. 100 BC; Isidore 2 (c. AD 1): 'a Greek city'; Tacitus Ann. 6.41 (AD 36): a Parthian town
ended_by: No named act: Greek is last attested c. AD 1
pre_greek_note: Isidore says the city was by then called Chalasar, a name known only from his Greek text; whether it was the older native name is unknown.
status_evidence: Isidore, Parthian Stations 2 ('a Greek city'); Strabo 16.1.17 (city of Apolloniatis); Apollodorus of Artemita; Cohen 2013
note: The site is not excavated and the identification with Karastel is not certain. Whether it was a Seleucid colony or a Hellenized native town (Chalasar) is unknown.
sources: Isidore of Charax, Parthian Stations 2; Strabo 16.1.17; Tacitus Ann. 6.41; Cohen 2013 (Artemita); Pleiades 894020

site: Babil, north of Hillah, Babil Governorate
greek_from_text: Antiochus IV settled a community of Greek citizens (politai) in Babylon c. 173/172 BC: the politai first appear in the Politai Chronicle (BCHP 13) in 172 BC, the Greek Community Chronicle (BCHP 14) says they 'entered Babylon at the command of Antiochus' and anointed themselves like the politai of Seleucia, and OGIS 253 (166 BC) calls Antiochus IV 'founder of the city'. Greeks had lived in Babylon since Alexander (331 BC), whose time the first theatre is dated to.
until_text: The politai appear in cuneiform texts until 77 BC; the Greek ephebic list of 111/110 BC (under Mithridates II) shows the gymnasium still active. A Greek inscription recording a repair of the theatre and its stage building by one Dioskourides is dated by its letter forms to the 2nd c. AD, the last evidence of the Greek community. Strabo (16.1.5) already calls Babylon largely deserted, and Trajan in 116 is said to have seen only mounds and ruins (Cassius Dio 68.30.1). The Greek community faded with the town itself.
fade_evidence: Politai in the astronomical diaries 169-77 BC; Greek ephebic victor list, 111/110 BC (Louvre); Graeco-Babyloniaca (cuneiform texts transcribed in Greek letters), 1st c. BC; last cuneiform tablet AD 79/80; Greek inscription for the repair of the theatre and its stage building, naming one Dioskouri[des], dated to the 2nd c. AD by its letter forms only (Livius: 'The Babylon theater inscription'); Trajan saw only mounds and ruins, 116 (Cassius Dio 68.30.1); Severus found Babylon deserted, 198 (Cassius Dio 76.9.3)
ended_by: No named act: the town declined after Seleucia drew away its people (Pliny 6.122; Strabo 16.1.5); the Greek community is last attested in the 2nd c. AD
other_language: Babylonian Akkadian (temple and scribal circles of the Esagila, written until AD 79/80) and Aramaic (common speech)
bilingual_evidence: A community of Greek citizens (politai) with its own gymnasium and theatre lived beside the Babylonian temple community; Greek ephebic victor list of 111/110 BC; Greek theatre-repair inscription of the 2nd c. AD
status_evidence: Greek politai, gymnasium and theatre (BCHP 13-14; OGIS 253; ephebic list of 111/110 BC); Alexander's capital
note: The Greek polis was a community of citizens inside a Babylonian city that kept its temple assembly, so it is classed as bilingual. Alexander died here in 323 BC.
sources: van der Spek 2005, 'Ethnic segregation in Hellenistic Babylon'; Livius: BCHP 14 (Greek Community Chronicle); Babylon theater inscription; OGIS 253; Cassius Dio 68.30; Pleiades 893951

other_names: Alexandria (Alexander); Antiochia (Antiochus IV); Karka d-Maishan (Syriac); Astarabad-Ardashir (Sasanian refoundation); Spasinou Charax
site: Jebel Khayabir (Naysan), north of Basra, Basra Governorate
greek_from_text: Alexander founded it as Alexandria in 324 BC on an artificial mound, settling invalid Macedonian soldiers and people from the royal town of Durine (Pliny 6.138); Antiochus IV refounded it as Antiochia after a flood, completed 166/165 BC; later Hyspaosines rebuilt its dykes and gave it his name (Pliny 6.139)
until_text: Greek administration ended when Hyspaosines, the Seleucid governor of Mesene, made himself king after 141 BC; the Greek language lived on under his dynasty, whose coins carry Greek legends: Hyspaosines (125-121 BC), Artabazos (48/47 BC) and Mithradates (AD 142/143). The geographer Isidore of Charax wrote in Greek c. AD 1. From the second half of the 2nd c. AD the coins are uninscribed or carry Aramaic legends in the local dialect. Ardashir I ended the kingdom in 221/222. No Greek-speaking community is attested in the Sasanian town.
fade_evidence: Isidore of Charax, Greek writer from the city, c. AD 1; Greek-legend coins of the kings of Characene to Mithradates (AD 142/143), then Aramaic legends from the later 2nd c. AD; Greek and Palmyrene inscriptions at Palmyra honouring the caravans and merchants of Spasinou Charax, 1st-2nd c. AD
ended_by: No named act for Greek speech: Ardashir I conquered Mesene in 221/222, killed its last king Bandu and refounded Charax as Astarabad-Ardashir (al-Tabari)
refounded_by: Antiochus IV (as Antiochia, 166/165 BC); Hyspaosines of Characene, governor from 166/165 BC and independent from c. 141-139 BC (as Spasinou Charax)
other_language: Aramaic, and Arabic in the Characene kingdom (Palmyrene and local Aramaic inscriptions; Aramaic legends replace Greek on the royal coins in the 2nd c. AD)
bilingual_evidence: Royal coins of Characene with Greek legends, later with Aramaic legends; a mixed population of Greeks, Aramaeans, Arabs and Palmyrene traders
status_evidence: Alexander foundation (Pliny 6.138-139); capital of Characene; royal coinage with Greek legends; Isidore of Charax
note: Greek city by foundation; how far Greek remained the main language under the Characene kings (2nd c. BC to 3rd c. AD) is uncertain. The site at Jebel Khayabir (Naysan), north of Basra, is now confirmed by the aerial, drone and geophysical surveys of Stefan Hauser's team (University of Konstanz), which mapped its walls, streets, canals and very large housing blocks.
sources: Pliny 6.138-139; Cohen 2013 (Alexandreia/Antiocheia/Charax Spasinou); Hansman 1967, 'Charax and the Karkheh'; Encyclopaedia Iranica: Characene; Hauser, Konstanz survey (reported in Archaeology, Feb. 2026); Pleiades 912872

other_names: Demetrias on the Tigris (coin legend 'of the Demetrians on the Tigris')
site: unlocated; Strabo puts it near Arbela (Erbil), the coins 'on the Tigris'; Erbil or Nineveh Governorate
greek_from_text: No source records the foundation: the name points to Demetrius I Soter (162-150 BC), perhaps after his victory over the rebel Timarchus c. 160 BC, or to Demetrius II (145-139 BC); the civic bronze coins of the 'Demetrians on the Tigris', with Tyche and tripod, belong to the same period if they are this city's
until_text: The civic coins belong to the Seleucid period; Assyria passed to Parthia and the kings of Adiabene from the 120s BC. Strabo (16.1.4, c. AD 20) still names Demetrias as a city near Arbela. Nothing later is known.
fade_evidence: Civic bronze coinage, 2nd c. BC; Strabo 16.1.4 (c. AD 20); Stephanus s.v. Demetrias
ended_by: No named act: no evidence after Strabo
status_evidence: Civic bronze coinage with Greek legend (DEMETRIEON TON PROS TOI TIGREI); Strabo 16.1.4 ('the city of Demetrias'); Stephanus
note: Site unknown; it may have been a refoundation of an Assyrian town. The 'on the Tigris' coins are usually given to this Demetrias, but they might belong to another city under a temporary dynastic name (Seleucia on the Tigris has been suggested); without them the city rests on Strabo and Stephanus alone.
sources: Strabo 16.1.4; Cohen 2013 (Demetrias in Assyria); Wikipedia: Demetrias in Assyria; Pleiades 876619

site: Kuyunjik and Nebi Yunus, east Mosul, Nineveh Governorate
greek_from_text: Resettled in the Seleucid period; Greek inscriptions, Greek cults and civic officials (strategos and epistates of the city) of the late Hellenistic and Parthian period
until_text: The Greek inscriptions belong to the 1st c. BC and the 1st c. AD; Damis, a Greek-writing companion of Apollonius of Tyana, came from Ninos in the 1st c. AD. Tacitus (Ann. 12.13) mentions the city in AD 49. No Greek evidence is known after the 2nd c. AD; the town lived on as an Aramaic-speaking Christian centre opposite Mosul.
fade_evidence: Greek civic inscriptions, 1st c. BC-1st c. AD (Reade 1998); Damis of Nineveh, 1st c. AD; marble Herakles Epitrapezios, 2nd c. AD; by 554 Nineveh was a see of the Church of the East, with Syriac as its language
ended_by: No named act: Greek is last attested in the 1st-2nd c. AD
bilingual_evidence: Greek inscriptions, one on a shrine of the Sebitti and one naming a strategos and epistates of the city; Greek sculpture (Hermes; Herakles Epitrapezios, 2nd c. AD); Damis of Nineveh, whose memoirs Philostratus says were written in Greek (Life of Apollonius 1.3, 1.19)
status_evidence: Seleucid refoundation as a polis with 'at least the superficial forms of Hellenistic city organization' (Oates 1968, 61); Greek inscriptions of the Parthian period naming a strategos and epistates of the city, and Greek dedications (Reade 1998); Greek sculpture (Herakles Epitrapezios); Damis of Ninos (Philostratus); Tacitus Ann. 12.13 (AD 49)
note: Nineveh was a small town after 612 BC; the Greek inscriptions show a Greek-style civic government in Parthian Adiabene, but the size of the Greek-speaking community is unknown. Philostratus' Damis may be a literary invention.
sources: Reade 1998, 'Greco-Parthian Nineveh', Iraq 60; Oates 1968, Studies in the Ancient History of Northern Iraq, 61; Gorgias Encyclopedic Dictionary of the Syriac Heritage: Nineveh; Invernizzi 1989 (Herakles Epitrapezios of Nineveh); Philostratus, Life of Apollonius 1.19; Pleiades 874621

other_names: Seleucia ad Tigrim (Latin); Seliq/Sliq, later Sliq Kharawta, 'ruined Seleucia' (Syriac), part of Mahoze; Coche was the quarter on the opposite bend where the Sasanian Veh-Ardashir rose c. 230
site: Tell Umar, near al-Mada'in (Salman Pak), Baghdad Governorate
greek_from_text: Seleucus I founded it on the Tigris near Opis as his eastern capital, c. 307-305 BC (Strabo 16.1.5; Pliny 6.122; Appian Syr. 58); Antiochus I moved settlers from Babylon there in 275/274 BC (Babylonian astronomical diary)
until_text: Greek administration ended when Mithridates I of Parthia took the city in 141 BC, but the polis lived on as a self-governing Greek city under Parthian rule: Tacitus (Ann. 6.42) praises its council of 300 and says it had 'not sunk into barbarism' but kept the ways of its founder. Its Greeks fought the Syrians and then, reconciled with them, massacred the city's Jews c. AD 35-40 (Josephus AJ 18.372-379) and held out against the Parthian kings in a seven-year revolt, AD 35-42 (Tacitus Ann. 11.8-9). Trajan's generals Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander burned it in 116 (Cassius Dio 68.30.2). In 165 the army of Avidius Cassius, under Lucius Verus, sacked and burned it after it had received the Romans as friends (Cassius Dio 71.2.3; HA Verus 8.3-4); Eutropius (8.10) and Orosius (7.15.3) speak of 400,000 people taken. When Septimius Severus came in 198 he found it deserted (Cassius Dio 76.9.3). The Sasanian city of Veh-Ardashir later rose beside the site, with no attested Greek-speaking community.
fade_evidence: Civic bronze coins with Greek legends (Tyche types), struck into the 1st c. AD; Greek and Parthian bilingual inscription on the bronze Herakles that Vologases IV set up in the temple of Apollo at Seleucia after conquering Mesene, AD 150/151; Greek ostraca and seal impressions from the excavations; deserted by 198 (Cassius Dio 76.9.3)
ended_by: Sacked and burned by the Roman army of Avidius Cassius under Lucius Verus, 165 (Cassius Dio 71.2.3; HA Verus 8.3-4), after Trajan's generals Erucius Clarus and Julius Alexander had burned it in 116 (Cassius Dio 68.30.2)
pre_greek_note: Built near the old town of Opis (Akkadian Upi), which it replaced; the exact relation of the two sites is uncertain.
other_language: Aramaic, spoken by the 'Syrians' of the city and by its Jewish community, beside Greek by the 1st c. AD
bilingual_evidence: Josephus (AJ 18.372-379) describes the Greeks and the Syrians as the two parties of the city c. AD 35-40, with the Jews siding with the Syrians
status_evidence: Seleucid royal foundation; council of 300 (Tacitus Ann. 6.42); civic coinage; 600,000 inhabitants in Pliny 6.122; Strabo 16.1.16
note: The largest Greek city of the East after Antioch and Alexandria. Treated as a Greek city with a bilingual period because Aramaic-speaking Syrians and Jews formed a large part of the population by the 1st c. AD.
sources: Cohen 2013 (Seleukeia on the Tigris); Tacitus Ann. 6.42, 11.8-9; Josephus AJ 18.372-379; Cassius Dio 68.30, 71.2, 76.9; Pleiades 894084

other_names: Uruk (Akkadian; Sumerian Unug); Erech (Hebrew Bible); Orchoe (Ptolemy 5.20.7); Orcheni, its astronomers (Strabo 16.1.6; Pliny 6.123); Warka (Arabic)
site: Tell al-Warka, Al-Muthanna Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek seal legends of the record office and Greek double names of residents from the late 3rd c. BC; no Greek civic institutions are attested
until_text: The last Greek text is an honorary decree found in the Gareus temple, which dates the temple to 422 of the Seleucid era, AD 110/111 (Meier 1960); a decree in Greek implies that the town's assembly still used Greek. The cuneiform temple culture ended in the 1st c. BC, and the Parthian town declined in the 2nd-3rd c. AD.
fade_evidence: Greek seal impressions of the record office, 3rd-2nd c. BC; Greek name of Anu-uballit Kephalon, 202/201 BC; Greek honorary decree from the Gareus temple, AD 110/111
ended_by: No named act: Greek is last attested at Uruk in AD 110/111; the town shrank and was largely deserted by early Sasanian times
other_language: Babylonian Akkadian (temple scribes and astronomers) and Aramaic
bilingual_evidence: Greek names in the leading Babylonian families (Anu-uballit Nikarchos, governor under Antiochus II; Anu-uballit Kephalon, builder of the Bit Resh, 202/201 BC); thousands of clay sealings with Greek seal legends of the city's record office (chreophylakes of Orchoi); a Greek honorary decree from the Gareus temple, AD 110/111
status_evidence: Ancient city with temple assembly; Greek record office (chreophylax) seal impressions; Greek honorary decree of AD 110/111; Ptolemy 5.20.7; Strabo 16.1.6
note: Whether more than a Hellenized elite spoke Greek at Uruk is debated; Greek double names may be honorific. Kept on the strength of the Greek record office and the Greek honorary decree of AD 110/111.
sources: Meier 1960, Greek honorary decree from the Gareus temple, Baghdader Mitteilungen 1; Kose 1998, Uruk: Architektur IV; Oelsner 2014 (Greek in Babylonia); Strabo 16.1.6; Pleiades 912986

site: Bushehr (proposed), Bushehr peninsula, Bushehr province (proposed; Rishahr and Tawwaj are other candidates)
greek_from_text: Founded or refounded by Antiochus I, probably while co-ruler with Seleucus I (c. 294-281 BC), with colonists sent at his request by Magnesia on the Maeander (OGIS 233).
until_text: Administration: Seleucid into the reign of Antiochus IV (royal coins struck there, 175-164 BC); Persis then passed to its own frataraka dynasts and under Parthian overlordship (c. 140 BC). Speech: the last evidence of the Greek city is the decree of 205 BC and the coins of Antiochus IV.
fade_evidence: Decree of the Antiochenes accepting the Leukophryena of Magnesia, 205 BC (OGIS 233; I.Magnesia 61); Seleucid royal coins of the mint of Antioch in Persis under Antiochus IV.
ended_by: No named act: Seleucid rule in Persis ended under the frataraka dynasts and Mithridates I of Parthia (c. 140 BC); nothing is known of the city later.
founder: Antiochus I (with colonists from Magnesia on the Maeander)
status_evidence: OGIS 233 (I.Magnesia 61): decree of the boule and demos, with executive magistrates and treasurers, 205 BC; Antiochus III's letter to Magnesia after receiving its envoys at Antioch in Persis (OGIS 231).
note: A full Greek polis whose site is unknown; Bushehr follows Pleiades and recent work. Rew-Ardashir (Rishahr), a Sasanian deportee town on the same peninsula, is a separate entry.
sources: OGIS 231 and 233; Cohen 2013 (Antiocheia in Persis); Rougemont 2012, IGIAC 53; Pleiades 922627

site: near Aradan (Khuvar/Choara), Garmsar area, Semnan province (proposed)
greek_from_text: Seleucid foundation named after Apama, wife of Seleucus I (c. 300-280 BC); one of the Macedonian foundations of Media in Strabo 11.13.6.
until_text: Administration: Seleucid until the Parthian advance into Choarene and Media in the 2nd c. BC (Mithridates I, c. 148/147 BC). Speech: no evidence of the Greek community after the Seleucid period; Isidore (late 1st c. BC) still names Apameia as a city.
fade_evidence: No inscriptions; known from Strabo, Pliny and Isidore only.
ended_by: No named act: the region passed to the Parthians, decisively under Mithridates I c. 148/147 BC.
status_evidence: Strabo 11.13.6 (Macedonian foundation); Pliny NH 6.43 (Apamea Rhagiane); Isidore of Charax 8 (city of Choarene).
note: Location unknown; the Barrington Atlas places it tentatively near Aradan with Choara, though Pliny keeps Apamea and Choara apart.
sources: Strabo 11.13.6; Isidore of Charax, Parthian Stations 8; Cohen 2013 (Apameia Rhagiane); Pleiades 942286

site: Bishapur ruins near Kazerun, Fars province
greek_from_text: Founded by Shapur I c. 266 and peopled in part with Roman captives (Chronicle of Seert).
until_text: Administration: Sasanian city and East-Syrian see; taken by the Arabs in the conquest of Fars (640s). Speech: no attestation of Greek speakers after the founding generation.
fade_evidence: Roman-style floor mosaics and Greek letters on Shapur I's monument (3rd c.); nothing later.
ended_by: No named act: assimilation of the deportees' descendants; the city fell in the Arab conquest of Fars in the 640s.
bilingual_evidence: Named by the Chronicle of Seert among the cities peopled with Shapur I's captives; Roman-style mosaics and Greek letters on Shapur I's monument point to Roman workmen.
status_evidence: Chronicle of Seert; Shapur I's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam; royal city of Shapur I.
note: Roman captives certainly worked there; a lasting Greek-speaking community is not directly attested.
sources: Chronicle of Seert (PO 4); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Deportations ii; Encyclopaedia Iranica: Bishapur; Pleiades 922740

site: Sarpol-e Zahab, Kermanshah Province (Iran), near the Iraqi border
greek_from_text: Isidore of Charax (Parthian Stations 3, late 1st c. BC) calls Chala 'a Greek city' in Chalonitis
until_text: Known as Greek only from Isidore. Later Hulwan was a Sasanian and early Islamic town on the Khorasan road, with no attested Greek speakers.
fade_evidence: Isidore 3 (late 1st c. BC/early 1st c. AD) is the only evidence
ended_by: No named act: no evidence after Isidore
status_evidence: Isidore, Parthian Stations 3 ('a Greek city'); Cohen 2013
note: Lies in Iran, just across the border from Iraq; included here because it sits on the road from Seleucia through Apolloniatis. The identification of Chala with Hulwan is usual but not certain.
sources: Isidore of Charax, Parthian Stations 3; Cohen 2013 (Chala); Pleiades 903043

other_names: Weh-Andiyok-Shabuhr, 'Shapur's better Antioch' (Middle Persian); Bet Lapat (Syriac); Bendosaboron (late Greek form); Jundaysabur (Arabic)
site: Shahabad (Eslamabad) village near Dezful, Khuzestan province
greek_from_text: Founded by Shapur I for captives from Antioch (taken 253 and/or 260) and named 'Shapur's better Antioch'; the archaeology shows no earlier settlement.
until_text: Administration: Sasanian city, later capital of Khuzistan and East-Syrian metropolitan see of Bet Huzaye; surrendered to the Arabs c. 638. Speech: the deportees' Greek is not recorded after the founding generations; their descendants merged into the Syriac- and Persian-speaking Church of the East, and teaching in the city's school was in Syriac.
fade_evidence: Chronicle of Seert on the Antiochene clergy and bishop Demetrianus (3rd c.); the synod of 410 already lists Bet Lapat as a Syriac see; no later attestation of Greek speakers.
ended_by: No named act: assimilation of the deportees' descendants; the city surrendered to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari's army c. 638.
bilingual_evidence: Founded for captives from Antioch; the Antiochene clergy elected a successor to their bishop Demetrianus there (Chronicle of Seert); deportee churches in Persis and Khuzistan used both Greek and Syriac.
status_evidence: Chronicle of Seert; Shapur I's inscription at Naqsh-e Rostam on the settlement of Roman captives; East-Syrian metropolitan see from 410.
note: The Greek-speaking community is inferred from the Antiochene origin of the settlers and the Chronicle of Seert; how long it kept Greek is unknown.
sources: Chronicle of Seert (PO 4); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Deportations ii; Encyclopaedia Iranica: Gondesapur; Pleiades 912873

site: Shahr-e Qumis, between Semnan and Damghan, Semnan province
greek_from_text: Named by Appian (Syr. 57) among the cities founded by Seleucus I in Parthyene; Curtius (6.2.15) calls it 'founded by Greeks' when Alexander arrived there in 330 BC.
until_text: Administration: Seleucid until Arsaces I's Parni took Parthyene c. 238 BC; Antiochus III recaptured Hecatompylos in 209 BC (Polybius 10.28) but left Parthia to Arsaces II; then a Parthian royal city. Speech: no evidence of a Greek-speaking community under Parthian rule.
fade_evidence: No Greek inscriptions; the excavated remains at Shahr-e Qumis are Parthian.
ended_by: Taken by Arsaces I of Parthia c. 238 BC; retaken by Antiochus III in 209 BC and left to the Parthians; no later trace of Greeks.
status_evidence: Appian, Syr. 57 (foundation of Seleucus I); Curtius 6.2.15; Polybius 10.28; Strabo 11.9.1.
note: The identification with Shahr-e Qumis is widely accepted but not proven; Curtius' 'founded by Greeks' for 330 BC is likely anachronistic.
sources: Appian, Syriaca 57; Curtius 6.2.15; Polybius 10.28; Cohen 2013 (Hekatompylos); Pleiades 942276

site: unlocated, in the Rey/Tehran plain, Tehran province (region only)
greek_from_text: Macedonian foundation near Rhagai (Strabo 11.13.6), early Seleucid period.
until_text: Administration: Seleucid until the Parthian conquest of Media under Mithridates I (c. 148/147 BC). Speech: nothing is known of the city after its mention by Strabo.
fade_evidence: None; known only from Strabo.
ended_by: No named act: Media conquered by Mithridates I of Parthia c. 148/147 BC.
status_evidence: Strabo 11.13.6 (one of the Greek cities founded by the Macedonians in Media).
note: Some link it with the Heraclea founded by Alexander and refounded by Antiochus as Achais (Pliny 6.48), which other sources put in Areia; the location is unknown and the point is a placeholder near Rhagai.
sources: Strabo 11.13.6; Cohen 2013 (Herakleia in Media); Pliny NH 6.48; Pleiades 906012 (Barrington Atlas map 92, unlocated Herakleia)

other_names: Niphaunda (Ptolemy); Nihavand (Middle Persian/Arabic); Mah al-Basra (early Islamic)
site: Nahavand, Hamadan province
greek_from_text: Founded by a King Antiochus (probably Antiochus I, 281-261 BC) and named after a queen Laodice; listed by Strabo (11.13.6) among the Macedonian foundations of Media.
until_text: Administration: Seleucid until Mithridates I of Parthia conquered Media c. 148/147 BC. Speech: the last evidence of the Greek city is the stele of 193 BC; nothing is known of it under Parthian rule.
fade_evidence: Stele of 193 BC (Menedemos to the magistrates and city of Laodicea, with Antiochus III's edict for the cult of Queen Laodice); a short honorary inscription for Menedemos, governor of the Upper Satrapies; an Ionic capital.
ended_by: No named act: Media conquered by Mithridates I of Parthia c. 148/147 BC; no later trace of the Greek community.
status_evidence: Strabo 11.13.6; Pliny NH 6; Nehavend stele of 193 BC: Menedemos' covering letter to Apollodotos and to the city of Laodicea (its archons and the city), with Antiochus III's ordinance on the cult of Queen Laodice (Robert 1949; Axon 1.2, 2017)
note: The stele, a chance find at Nahavand, fixes the location; the Kermanshah copy of the same edict comes from a different place.
sources: Strabo 11.13.6; Robert, Hellenica 7 (1949); Cohen 2013 (Laodikeia in Media); Iranohellenica: Nahavand (Laodicea); Pleiades 903088

site: Rishahr, south of Bushehr city, Bushehr province
greek_from_text: Roman captives settled by Shapur I after his campaigns of 253-260 in a town founded by Ardashir I (Chronicle of Seert).
until_text: Administration: Sasanian; metropolitan see of Fars from 424; taken by the Arabs in the early 640s. Speech: the 'Roman' church with Greek liturgy is recorded for the deportee generations only; later bishops of Rew-Ardashir worked in Syriac and Persian.
fade_evidence: Chronicle of Seert on the Roman and Carmanian churches (3rd c.); metropolitan see of Fars at the synod of 424 (Syriac); no later attestation of Greek speakers.
ended_by: No named act: assimilation of the deportees' descendants; Uthman ibn Abi al-As defeated the governor Shahrak at Rishahr and took the town in the early 640s (al-Baladhuri).
pre_greek_note: The town predates the arrival of the deportees by a few decades; earlier occupation on the Bushehr peninsula goes back to the Elamite period (Liyan).
bilingual_evidence: The Chronicle of Seert says the deportees built two churches there, one for the Romans and one for the Carmanians, with liturgy in Greek and Syriac.
status_evidence: Chronicle of Seert: a church of the Roman captives beside a church of the Carmanians, with the liturgy in Greek and in Syriac (the Gorgias Encyclopedic Dictionary of the Syriac Heritage, 'Fars', calls the report of a Greek and Syriac liturgy in 3rd-c. Fars plausible); East-Syrian metropolitan see of Fars (424)
note: The Hellenistic Antioch in Persis may have stood on the same peninsula; the two are kept apart because both sites are uncertain and the communities are five centuries apart. A second Rew-Ardashir/Reishahr, near Arrajan on the Fars-Khuzestan border, is also known; the metropolitan see and the deportee town are usually placed on the Bushehr peninsula.
sources: Chronicle of Seert (PO 4); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Deportations ii; Gorgias Encyclopedic Dictionary of the Syriac Heritage: Fars; Pleiades 922711

other_names: Ragā (Old Persian, Bisotun inscription); Rages (Book of Tobit); Europos (Seleucus I); Arsakia (Parthian); Ray/Rey (Persian, Arabic)
site: Rey, south of Tehran, Tehran province
greek_from_text: Refounded by Seleucus I Nicator as Europos, c. 300 BC (Strabo 11.13.6).
until_text: Administration: Seleucid until the Parthian conquest of Media under Mithridates I (c. 148/147 BC); the Parthians renamed the city Arsakia. Speech: no evidence of Greek speakers after the conquest; Isidore of Charax calls Rhaga the largest city of Media.
fade_evidence: No Greek inscriptions known; the Parthian renaming Arsakia (Strabo 11.13.6).
ended_by: Taken by Mithridates I of Parthia c. 148/147 BC and renamed Arsakia; no later trace of Greeks.
bilingual_evidence: Refounded by Seleucus I as Europos, named after his Macedonian home town, and counted by Strabo among the Greek cities founded by the Macedonians; the old Median town of Ragā remained a large native centre.
status_evidence: Strabo 11.13.6 (founded by Nicator as Europos; Macedonian foundation); Isidore of Charax 7.
note: Classed bilingual because Europos was a refoundation of a large Median town; Strabo is the only evidence for the Macedonian settlers.
sources: Strabo 11.13.6; Isidore of Charax, Parthian Stations 7; Cohen 2013 (Europos/Rhagai); Encyclopaedia Iranica: Ray; Pleiades 903104

site: unlocated, in ancient Hyrcania (Golestan or Mazandaran province)
greek_from_text: First and only evidence: Greeks living in the city at Antiochus III's siege, 209 BC (Polybius 10.31); the community probably dated from the early Seleucid period.
until_text: Administration: Hyrcania was under the Parthians from c. 235 BC; Antiochus III took Sirynx in 209 BC and then left the region to Arsaces II. Speech: the Greek residents were massacred by the defenders before the city fell.
fade_evidence: Polybius 10.31 (siege of 209 BC).
ended_by: The Greek residents were killed by the city's native and Parthian defenders during Antiochus III's siege, 209 BC (Polybius 10.31).
bilingual_evidence: Polybius (10.31) says that when Antiochus III's siege was about to succeed, the native defenders killed the Greeks living in the city, a resident Greek community.
status_evidence: Polybius 10.31 (a strong city of Hyrcania with Greek residents).
note: A Greek minority in a fortified Hyrcanian city; how large it was, and whether it ever formed a civic body, is unknown. Location unknown; the point marks the Hyrcanian plain.
sources: Polybius 10.31; Walbank, Historical Commentary on Polybius II, on 10.31

greek: Σοῦσα, Σελεύκεια ἡ πρὸς τῷ Εὐλαίῳ
other_names: Šušan/Šušun (Elamite); Shushan (Hebrew Bible); Seleucia on the Eulaios (Seleucid); 'the city of the Phraateans in Susa', after Phraates IV refounded it c. 31/30 BC (Greek inscriptions); Shush (Persian), al-Sus (Arabic)
site: Shush, Khuzestan province
greek_from_text: Greco-Macedonian settlers under the early Seleucids; the city was refounded as Seleucia on the Eulaios by a Seleucid king (Seleucus I or Antiochus I?), the exact date uncertain; Greek inscriptions from the 3rd c. BC.
until_text: Administration: Seleucid until c. 147-140 BC; Elymaean kings seized the city briefly and Mithridates I of Parthia took it from them c. 140 BC; Parthians held it to at least AD 45, then Elymaean kings from the later 1st c. AD; Sasanian from 224. Speech: the Greek polis kept its institutions under Parthian rule (Artabanus II confirmed the election of the city treasurer Hestiaios in AD 21), but Greek traditions weakened and disappeared under Elymaean rule from the later 1st c. AD (Encyclopaedia Iranica). No dated Greek inscription is later than the early 1st c. AD.
fade_evidence: Greek dedications and manumissions of the 2nd-1st c. BC; two epigrams for the irrigation official Zamaspes (first decade of the 1st c. AD); letter of Artabanus II to the magistrates, December AD 21 (SEG 7.1); a Greek hymn to Apollo of the 1st c. AD; no later dated Greek text (Encyclopaedia Iranica: Epigraphy ii).
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. Taken by Mithridates I of Parthia c. 140 BC; Greek civic life faded after the Elymaean kings took Susa in the later 1st c. AD; taken by the Sasanian Ardashir I in 224; razed by Shapur II in the 4th c. (Syriac and Arabic tradition).
founder: a Seleucid king (refoundation as Seleucia; Seleucus I or Antiochus I?)
other_language: Aramaic and the local Elamite/Iranian speech of the native population
bilingual_evidence: A Greek polis (Seleucia on the Eulaios) with council, assembly, archons, treasurers and gymnasium, living beside a large native population with Iranian, Semitic and Elamite names; about fifty Greek inscriptions (dedications, manumissions to Nanaia, epigrams).
status_evidence: Greek civic institutions (boule, archons, treasurers, gymnasium) in Greek inscriptions (Rougemont, IGIAC 1-50); letter of Artabanus II to the city, AD 21; Seleucid mint.
note: Greek polis inside a large native town; classed bilingual. The Greek community lasted at least into the early 1st c. AD.
sources: Cohen 2013 (Seleukeia on the Eulaios); Rougemont 2012, IGIAC 1-50; Encyclopaedia Iranica: Susa iv; SEG 7.1; Pleiades 912936
